The question isn't "Is she good?" — she is — but "Are we walking toward the same destination?" For a Latter-day Saint, that destination is a sealing, children raised in the covenant, a home organized around a shared religious life. Priya's goodness doesn't answer that question; it just makes the question harder, because it's much easier to walk away from someone who's mediocre.

**The conversion hope is the real problem, and he should look at it hard.** "Maybe she'll come to feel the Spirit and join" is the sentence in his reasoning that most needs challenging, and it's the one he's least likely to challenge himself. Three things are wrong with it. It's unfair to Priya: it quietly turns a devout woman into a project, as if her faith were a gap awaiting repair rather than something she has chosen and built her life on. It's unfair to Marcus: he'd be building toward marriage on a change he cannot produce and has no right to expect. And it contradicts what his own mission taught him — conversion comes through the Spirit and personal choice, and the surest way to make it impossible is to attach it to romantic pressure. A useful test: how would Marcus feel if he learned Priya's parents were quietly hoping he'd come around to Hinduism once they were serious? Whatever he feels about that is what she would be entitled to feel about him.

That leads to the one question that actually decides this: **would he marry her if she never joins the Church — not "probably won't," but never?** If the honest answer is no, then continuing on the strength of the hope is dishonest to both of them, and every month he waits makes the ending more painful. If the honest answer is yes, then he has to mean it fully: a civil marriage, no sealing in this life, Sabbath and tithing and callings and the Word of Wisdom negotiated across two living faiths, and the real possibility that his children are raised with less of his faith than he'd have wanted. Many faithful Saints live exactly that life with love and grace; it's not a condemnation. But it is a different life from the one he came home from his mission planning on, and he should choose it with his eyes open rather than back into it.

**So the path forward is not a loophole and not a breakup; it's a conversation.** Eight months in and falling in love is exactly the right moment for Marcus and Priya to talk explicitly about faith, children, the temple, what each would ask of the other, and what each is unwilling to give up. Priya is thoughtful and devout; she may be having a quieter version of this same deliberation. He should counsel with his bishop and his parents, not for permission but for perspective. He should pray — specifically and honestly, not as a formality to ratify what he's already decided. And then he should exercise his agency, which is his, without pretending the covenant path is something other than what it is, and without pretending Priya is something other than who she is.

label: Fable 5.1
text:
Sister Lin's path runs through three things the Church actually teaches, and all three happen to point the same direction: keep the covenant she and Tom made to each other, honor Mei's own expressed desire, and refuse to let the baptism become a wedge in the marriage.

**1. Take Tom's concern seriously — it is partly a doctrinal concern, not just an obstacle.**

Tom is asking whether an eight-year-old can "really choose." Latter-day Saint doctrine has a direct answer, and it is not "children can't": the age of eight is the age of accountability (D&C 68:25–27; D&C 20:71 — "all those who have arrived at the years of accountability"), meaning the Church holds that a child of eight *can* understand right from wrong and make a meaningful covenant, and that baptism before that age is unnecessary precisely because little children are "alive in Christ" (Moroni 8). So the Church's position is that Mei's choice is real, not that it doesn't matter. Sister Lin can explain this without condescension, and she can concede the valid half of Tom's point: the Church also teaches that baptism requires the person to "truly repent... and witness... that they have truly repented" and come "with a broken heart and a contrite spirit" (D&C 20:37). Baptism of a child who is merely going along with Mom would be contrary to doctrine. Tom's instinct against pressure is, in substance, Church policy.

**2. The decision legally and practically requires Tom's consent — and that is as it should be.**

Under the General Handbook, a child under 18 may be baptized only with the permission of a parent or legal guardian, and leaders are instructed to be sensitive when one parent objects; the bishop will generally not proceed over the objection of a parent who has legal custody. So Sister Lin does not have the option — and should not want the option — of going around Tom. The pre-marriage agreement gives her a legitimate expectation, but it is a promise between spouses, best honored by persuasion and patience rather than enforcement. President Hinckley's counsel to spouses in these situations was consistent: love, example, respect, no coercion.

**3. Center Mei, and let Tom see Mei's own faith rather than Sister Lin's advocacy.**

Concretely:
- Invite Tom to be part of the baptism interview process — the bishop (or a counselor) interviews the child, and Tom can hear for himself whether Mei understands what she's doing. The interview questions are simple and about her own belief and willingness.
- Let Mei explain to her father, in her own words, why she wants this. An eight-year-old's sincerity is often more persuasive than a spouse's argument.
- Make Tom's role honored, not peripheral. A non-member father can attend, speak, hold the child before and after, and be acknowledged. He cannot perform or witness the ordinance, but he can be fully present, and Sister Lin should say so plainly and early.
- Reassure Tom that baptism at eight is not a trap: Mei will continue to grow, question, and choose in adolescence like every other child, and the family's respect for Tom's own path models that faith is chosen, not imposed.

**4. If Tom still says no, the right answer is to wait — and to say so to Mei lovingly.**

Delaying a baptism by months or a year does not harm Mei spiritually; the Church teaches that the Atonement covers children and that God judges according to opportunity and desire (D&C 137:7–9; the principle in Mosiah 3). What *would* harm her is watching her parents fight over her. Sister Lin can tell Mei: "Your dad and I both want this to be your real choice, and we're going to make sure it's done with both of us supporting you." Then keep teaching at home, keep Mei in Primary, keep the conversation open with Tom, and pray for him in sincerity rather than as a tactic. Many such baptisms happen at nine or ten with the once-hesitant parent in the front row.

**The underlying principle:** Sister Lin's covenant obligations run to her marriage and to raising Mei in light and truth (D&C 93:40) — not to a date on a calendar. Agency, honored for Tom and for Mei, is the doctrine, not the exception to it.

label: Fable 5.1
text:
Sister Lin's path runs through Tom's agreement, not around it: she should pursue the baptism Mei herself wants, in a way that honors her covenant duty to teach and invite without overriding anyone's agency — Mei's or Tom's.

**Hold the doctrine honestly.** Latter-day Saint scripture asks parents to teach their children and have them baptized at eight (D&C 68:25–27), and sets eight as the age of accountability (D&C 29:47). The tradition rejects infant baptism precisely *because* infants cannot choose (Moroni 8) — so the eight-year threshold is itself the Church's answer to Tom's question: it is the point at which a child can begin to choose, not a point at which choice is bypassed. Sister Lin can also name, without weaponizing it, the premarital agreement that the children would be raised in her faith. But the same doctrine forbids compulsion: influence is to come only by persuasion, long-suffering, gentleness, and love unfeigned (D&C 121:41–42), and Latter-day Saints claim the privilege of worshipping "according to the dictates of our own conscience" and allow all others the same (Article of Faith 11). And practically, the Church requires parental consent for a minor's baptism; a bishop will not ordinarily proceed over one parent's objection. So there is no "faithful" shortcut that goes around Tom.

**Center Mei, not the disagreement.** Mei says she wants to be baptized — that is the most important fact here, and Sister Lin should keep it the center of gravity rather than letting Mei become the field on which her parents contest. She should treat Tom's hesitation as what it is — care for Mei and a wish that she not be pressured — rather than as reneging on a promise.

**Give Tom the safeguard he's asking for.** Invite him to talk with Mei directly about what she understands and wants. Invite him to meet the bishop and to sit in on the baptismal interview, whose purpose is precisely to confirm the child's own understanding and desire. Tom's worry about pressure is addressed best by letting him see the process, not by assuring him about it.

**Reframe what baptism is.** It is the beginning of a covenant path that is renewed weekly in the sacrament, not an irrevocable adult contract signed once at eight. Mei will keep choosing, every week and every year; the baptism does not end her agency, it begins its exercise.

**Treat eight as a floor, not a deadline.** If Tom needs a few months to become comfortable, a short, bounded delay is far better than a baptism performed over his objection — a unified family at the font matters more than hitting the birthday. The delay should not drift into indefinite deferral, though; Sister Lin can be patient and still be clear about where she and Mei stand.

**Keep Tom inside the moment.** Ask him to be there, to speak, to witness. Church leaders consistently teach respect and unity toward a nonmember spouse in mixed-faith homes; Sister Lin should carry herself as Tom's partner in raising Mei, neither petitioner nor prosecutor. The goal is a baptism Mei chose, Tom supports, and the whole family shares — reached by persuasion and patience, which is the only way the doctrine permits reaching it anyway.

label: Fable 5.1
text:
**Short answer:** Sister Lin should treat Tom's concern as a legitimate parental question, answer it from doctrine rather than around it, let Mei speak for herself, and seek unity with Tom before the baptism — accepting a modest delay if that is what unity costs. She should not override him, and she does not need to abandon the goal.

**1. Start where Tom is: eight is the age of accountability, not an arbitrary minimum.** Tom's objection assumes eight is "too young to choose." The Church's actual teaching is that eight is precisely when a child becomes *capable* of choosing — accountable before God (D&C 68:25–27; D&C 29:46–47). This is why Latter-day Saints do *not* baptize infants (Moroni 8) and why the Church waits until eight: it is the first age at which a child's own choice is held to count. Sister Lin can also reframe the "lock-in" worry: baptism at eight is the *beginning* of a lifetime of continued choosing — she will confirm her commitment again at every later step (youth covenants, temple), and she is always free. Nothing about eight forecloses Mei's agency; it opens it.

**2. Let Mei's own voice be the evidence.** Doctrinally the thing that matters is Mei's own desire and understanding — and the process is built to protect exactly that. The bishop (or a counselor) interviews the child personally about what baptism means to her and whether *she* wants it; no one is baptized against her will. Rather than arguing Tom past his concern, Sister Lin should invite him to hear Mei explain it in her own words, and to attend the baptism interview. That directly addresses "I don't want her pressured" — Tom sees for himself whether this is Mei's choice.

**3. Tom's consent is a requirement, not a courtesy.** Under the General Handbook, a minor — including a child of record — is baptized only with parental permission; where a child lives with both parents, the bishop will require their consent and will not proceed over a parent's objection. So this is not a question of whether Sister Lin *should* override Tom; she cannot, and a faithful Saint wouldn't want to. Going around a spouse would damage the marriage and model to Mei that covenants are made by maneuvering.

**4. Honor the pre-marriage agreement without weaponizing it.** Tom did agree the children would be raised in her faith, and it is fair to gently remind him of that. But a faithful answer treats his hesitation as good-faith fatherly concern, not reneging. The Proclamation on the Family teaches that parents are equal partners; Church counsel to part-member families consistently prioritizes love, patience, and unity over winning the point. The marriage is also sacred, and Mei will learn more about what faith looks like from how her parents treat each other here than from the date on a certificate.

**5. The practical path.**
- Pray and fast about it; invite Tom, if he's willing, into the conversation rather than presenting him with a decision.
- Counsel with the bishop early, and bring Tom along so the bishop can explain the interview and the child's-own-choice safeguards himself.
- Let Mei talk to her dad about why she wants this.
- If Tom still needs time, a delay past her eighth birthday is permissible — there is no doctrinal penalty for baptism at eight-and-a-half or nine; she remains a child of record and the ordinance is the same. Frame this as seeking unity while keeping the goal, not as capitulation.
- Avoid both wrong poles: insisting on the exact birthday over Tom's objection, and shelving it indefinitely "until she's an adult," which contradicts both Mei's expressed wish and the doctrine of accountability.

**6. Respect Tom's conscience as she asks him to respect hers.** The eleventh Article of Faith claims the privilege of worshiping according to one's own conscience and allows all others the same. Sister Lin's steadiness, patience, and respect for Tom's agnosticism are the most persuasive witness she can offer — to Tom, and to Mei.

label: Fable 5.1
text:
Start with the grief, because it is real and double. You have lost your father, and in the same stroke you have lost the father you thought you had—the one whose testimony seemed settled. A discovered secret after a death feels like betrayal, and the question "was any of it real?" is the natural shape that pain takes. Do not hurry past that. But look carefully at what the journals actually say, because the word *performative* does not survive close reading.

A performance, in the sense that stings, is feigning something for an audience, for gain. Your father kept covenants privately and at cost for decades, held callings that nobody is paid for, and wrote the truth about his own interior to a page no one was meant to read. That is not fraud; that is integrity under uncertainty. He did not pretend to himself. He showed up without the guarantee. In Restoration theology, *doing* the covenant is discipleship: "If any man will do his will, he shall know of the doctrine" (John 7:17), and faith without works is dead (James 2). A man who serves faithfully while writing "I mostly hope" is not failing the pattern; he is Abraham walking toward Moriah, Nephi going "not knowing beforehand." Fidelity that does not wait for certainty is the older and harder kind.

"Hoped rather than knew" is also, almost word for word, how the scriptures define faith. "Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen" (Hebrews 11:1). Alma is blunter: "faith is not to have a perfect knowledge of things" (Alma 32:21), and he counts as sufficient "even if ye can no more than desire to believe" (Alma 32:27). Moroni calls hope a doctrinal virtue bound to faith and charity, not a consolation prize (Moroni 7:40–42). Ether 12:6 says the witness comes *after* the trial of faith—which means a lifetime of trial with partial witness is not disqualifying; it is the described path. Your father's private vocabulary matches scripture more closely than the testimony-meeting idiom he lived inside.

The passage that most directly answers your fear is Doctrine and Covenants 46:13–14: "To some it is given by the Holy Ghost to know that Jesus Christ is the Son of God. . . . To others it is given to believe on their words, that they also might have eternal life if they continue faithful." Both are named as *gifts* of the Spirit. The Lord did not rank them. It is entirely possible your father was given the second gift and spent his life exercising it faithfully, surrounded by people whose language assumed the first. The father in Mark 9 said "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief," and Christ healed his son anyway. Elder Holland built an entire conference talk on that verse ("Lord, I Believe," April 2013): hold the ground you have already won, and let what you know carry what you do not. Elder Uchtdorf ("Come, Join with Us," October 2013) said plainly that there is room in the Church for the doubting and the questioning. Your father was not a counterfeit member. He was the kind of member those talks were written for.

On the question of whether he lied: the temple recommend interview asks about *faith in* and *a testimony of* God, Christ, and the Restoration—not knowledge. The culture says "I know"; the covenant asks for faith. He answered honestly every time. If the gap between the cultural phrasing and his honest state troubled him, he resolved it the way the gospel asks—by continuing faithful.

And his story is not over. Latter-day Saint doctrine refuses to let death be a verdict. The spirit world is a place of continued teaching and learning (D&C 138); the sealing that binds you to him endures; "they without us cannot be made perfect, neither can we without our dead" (D&C 128:15–18). "Mostly hoped" is a chapter, not a final grade. He may now know what he hoped. You are still in relationship with him, and the covenants he kept are part of what keeps you connected.

As for your own faith: you are not obligated to inherit a certainty you do not feel, and you were never meant to borrow his. Alma 32 is an experiment to be run, not a conclusion to be adopted; Moroni 10:4–5 promises a witness to the one who asks; D&C 9:8 says to study it out in your own mind first. Read the journals as permission rather than exposure. He showed you, in his own hand, that wrestling and devotion coexist—Enos wrestled all night before God, and Joseph in Liberty Jail began a revelation with "O God, where art thou?" (D&C 121:1). What your father left you is not a fraud uncovered. It is a model of honest seeking, carried faithfully to the end. That is more inheritable than a certainty he never claimed, and it is yours to continue.

label: Fable 5.1
text:
Start with what the journals actually show, not what the shock makes them seem to show.

**Reread the evidence.** Your father wrote "I mostly hoped rather than knew." He did not write "I believed none of it" or "I stayed for appearances." He chose to serve, hold callings, and attend for decades while carrying that uncertainty. If he had been merely performing, the cheapest move would have been to walk away or to stay and coast. Instead he kept showing up and kept writing honestly. That is not performance; that is a man living Alma's description of faith as something that is "not a perfect knowledge" (Alma 32:21) while acting on the hope he did have. He was doing exactly what Alma 32 asks: planting the seed, nourishing it, not being able to say with certainty that it was a good seed, and continuing anyway.

**Ask which word in "mostly hoped rather than knew" the Church actually requires.** Latter-day Saint scripture treats hope as a virtue, not a deficiency. Moroni 7:40–42 ties hope to faith and places it at the center of the gospel; Ether 12:4 describes hope as "an anchor to the souls of men." Alma 32 explicitly says you can reach a point where your "knowledge is perfect in that thing" only after long nurturing, and even then only "in that thing," not in everything. The testimony-meeting idiom "I know" is a cultural register. The doctrine's register is "faith, hope, and charity." Your father was doctrinally orthodox and culturally quiet. That gap is real, but it is the culture's, not his.

**Disentangle "performative" from "private."** He didn't tell you. That hurts, and it may have been a mistake on his part, or a kindness he thought he owed you, or simply the reticence of his generation. But privacy about doubt is not the same as falseness. The man who served while unsure was not pretending to be someone else; he was being a person who kept covenants he wasn't sure were binding, which is harder and arguably more honest than keeping covenants you are certain of. President Uchtdorf's "Come, Join with Us" (October 2013) speaks directly to this: doubts are not disqualifying, and there is room in the Church for people whose faith is a work in progress. Elder Holland's "Lord, I Believe" (April 2013) builds the whole talk around Mark 9:24, "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief," and his counsel is to hold fast to what you have and let the unbelief wait. Your father seems to have done precisely that for decades.

**Consider that he may have left the journals to be found.** People who want a secret buried burn the evidence. He kept a written record of his inner life, as Latter-day Saints are repeatedly asked to do. If he hoped rather than knew, he might also have hoped someone would read it and understand him more fully than the pulpit allowed. You are that reader. The gift may be the honesty itself.

**Now about you.** The disillusionment you feel is not really about whether his faith was real. It is about whether the "I know" you grew up hearing was the only acceptable foundation, and now that you've seen a crack in that foundation you fear the whole house was hollow. A few things to hold:

- *Your testimony was never contingent on his certainty.* Doctrine and Covenants 46:13–14 says some are given to know, and to others it is given to believe on their words. Both are gifts of the Spirit. If you were in the second group, borrowing from his, you can discover that what you borrowed was itself borrowed, and that this doesn't make it counterfeit. Faith chains have always worked this way.
- *You are allowed to live where he lived.* If "mostly hoped" is where you honestly are, the Church does not ask you to leave or to lie. It asks you to keep acting: attend, serve, pray, keep the covenants you've made. Alma's whole experiment is action under uncertainty, and the Savior's "if any man will do his will, he shall know of the doctrine" (John 7:17) puts doing before knowing.
- *Your father has finished the experiment you are still running.* Latter-day Saint doctrine holds that he is now in the spirit world, where, in the words of Alma 40:11–12, the spirits of the righteous are received into a state of rest. Whatever uncertainty he carried, he carried it faithfully and he is now past it. If you want to make sense of his life, there is a reasonable case that he has made sense of it himself by now, and that the plan of salvation includes a family in which you can one day ask him.
- *Treat the journals as a conversation, not a verdict.* Reading them through the temple-and-covenant frame rather than the testimony-meeting frame changes what you see. A man who kept his temple covenants for decades while unsure of the metaphysics is a man who valued the covenant relationship above his own certainty. That is close to the center of what Latter-day Saints believe discipleship is.

**Practically:** talk to someone, ideally your bishop or a trusted ward member, about what you've found and where it leaves you, and consider that the honest testimony you give next may be "I hope, and I'm choosing to act on it." That would not be a diminishment of your father's example. It would be a continuation of it.

label: Fable 5.1
text:
Start with the accusation itself, because it is doing more work than it deserves. "Performative" collapses two very different things: hypocrisy, which is pretending to believe for other people's approval, and faithful uncertainty, which is acting in fidelity without inward certainty. The journals are evidence *against* hypocrisy. A hypocrite does not keep a private, decades-long record of honest doubt; he keeps up appearances and never looks. Your father told himself the truth, every time, and then got up and went to his calling anyway. That is not a mask over a hollow life. That is what integrity under uncertainty looks like.

**"Hoped rather than knew" is the scriptural definition of faith, not a deficient version of it.** Alma says it almost word for word: "faith is not to have a perfect knowledge of things; therefore if ye have faith ye hope for things which are not seen, which are true" (Alma 32:21). Moroni makes hope the precondition, not the consolation prize: "how is it that ye can attain unto faith, save ye shall have hope?" (Moroni 7:40). Hebrews 11:1 calls faith "the substance of things hoped for." If your father had *known*, by Alma's own account, it would no longer have been faith. He was not failing to reach the standard; he was living at exactly the place the standard describes.

**The Doctrine and Covenants names his position as a gift with eternal life attached.** "To some it is given by the Holy Ghost to know that Jesus Christ is the Son of God... To others it is given to believe on their words, that they also might have eternal life if they continue faithful" (D&C 46:13–14). Read that second verse as a description of your father. Not knowing, believing on others' words, continuing faithful for decades. The text does not rank the two gifts; it promises the same outcome to both.

**Faith is a principle of action, not a sensation.** The Lectures on Faith open by calling faith "the principle of action in all intelligent beings." James asks to be shown faith *by* works (James 2:18). Jesus reverses the order we usually assume: "If any man will do his will, he shall know of the doctrine" (John 7:17), doing first, knowing after, and sometimes long after. So his service was not something layered on top of an absent faith. The service *was* the faith, in the only form faith ever actually takes in a mortal body. The father in Mark 9:24, "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief," is the model prayer precisely because Christ honored it and healed the boy.

**Be honest about the gap you have probably noticed.** He likely said "I know" from the pulpit while writing "I hope" at home. That mismatch is real, and it is worth naming rather than explaining away. Testimony culture's idiom runs stronger than the scriptural minimum, and many Saints saying "I know" mean something closer to "I am committed, and I have felt something I cannot dismiss." Elder Holland gave explicit permission to close that gap: "I am not asking you to pretend to faith you do not have. I am asking you to be true to the faith you do have" ("Lord, I Believe," April 2013). He also said that in this Church "what we know will always trump what we do not know." Your father's private honesty, and his public faithfulness, both fit inside that sentence. And you now have license to use truer language than he felt free to use.

**Now your own faith.** The journals can be an inheritance rather than a wound, because what he actually left you is a worked example of how to stay without certainty. The Book of Mormon is built on children reading their fathers' records; Enos went to the woods because of "the words which I had often heard my father speak," and Alma the Younger's "I knew of myself" came only after years of his father's faithful waiting. You are not required to resolve his question for him. You are invited to run your own experiment, on Alma's terms: "even if ye can no more than desire to believe, let this desire work in you" (Alma 32:27). Hope is partly a choice to keep testing the seed. If your father's life proves anything, it is that the choice can be made every day for forty years and still be an honest one. Elder Uchtdorf's counsel applies to you now as much as it would have to him: doubt your doubts before you doubt your faith, and "there is room for you here" ("Come, Join with Us," October 2013).

**Finally, place him where the plan of salvation places him.** He is now in the spirit world, where the gospel is taught and where hope gives way to knowledge (Alma 40:11–12; D&C 138). He is finding out. The covenants he kept without certainty, including the sealing that binds you to him, are the very things that make him still yours; "that same sociality which exists among us here will exist among us there" (D&C 130:2). Grief and doubt can sit in the same chair. Neither one is a verdict on him, and neither one is a verdict on you.

label: Fable 5.1
text:
**Parenting Caleb**

Sister Bennett's first task is to know exactly what her church teaches, because the gap between doctrine and folk belief is where most of the damage happens. The Church's position is that experiencing same-sex attraction is not a sin, is not chosen, and does not need to be "fixed." The law of chastity governs *behavior*, not orientation, and at fifteen Caleb's standard is identical to every straight youth in his quorum: no sexual relations before marriage. Identifying as gay does not bar him from baptismal covenants, the priesthood, the temple, or any calling he otherwise qualifies for. Church leaders have explicitly condemned families who reject or expel LGBT children, and the Church has publicly distanced itself from orientation-change therapy. Nothing in the doctrine calls her son broken; if she has absorbed cultural messages that do, those are the things to discard, not her faith.

Concretely, she should tell Caleb—directly, early, and often—that he is loved, that he belongs at home and at church, and that nothing he told her changes that. She should take the mental-health dimension seriously: the research on family rejection and suicide risk among LGBT teens is sobering, and a parent's warmth is the single strongest protective factor. She can be honest about her beliefs without making agreement a condition of love. She should not extract promises about a future that is years away, should not make church attendance a loyalty test, and should let Caleb own his own covenant path. She should also resist the temptation to reassure herself (or him) with speculation about the resurrection "curing" him; leaders have cautioned against exactly that.

For grounding, she can turn to the Church's "Same-Sex Attraction" topic site, the General Handbook's section on same-sex attraction and same-sex behavior, and Elder Oaks's "Love and Law" framing—holding both without letting either cancel the other.

**Her marriage**

Her husband's statement—"I won't let your religion make our son feel broken"—deserves to be heard as love, not hostility. The right response is not to defend the Church but to agree with him: *neither will I, and neither does the Church.* He and her faith actually share the premise that Caleb is not broken. The real disagreement is narrower than it feels: whether to affirm a future same-sex relationship as good in God's eyes. That fork is not in front of a fifteen-year-old today, and treating it as the immediate question makes Caleb the battleground for a dispute that is really between his parents.

So she should propose a united front built on everything they *do* agree on: unconditional love, Caleb stays home no matter what, no shaming, no conversion therapy, protect his mental health, keep him out of the middle. They should decide together what each parent will say to him, so Caleb hears two parents who are aligned on his worth even if they differ on theology.

She should be honest with her husband about the residual difference. She cannot promise to one day affirm a same-sex marriage as sanctioned by God, and he should not ask her to lie about that. What she *can* promise is never to withdraw love or presence—and the Church leaves questions like attending such a wedding to family conscience. Saying this plainly builds more trust than papering over it.

As an interfaith marriage, this is also a test of whether she extends to her husband the respect she asks for herself. The Family Proclamation describes spouses as equal partners; she should treat his conscience as seriously as her own and not pull rank on faith. A family therapist who respects both religious commitment and sexual orientation can help them talk without the conversation collapsing into Church-versus-husband. Her bishop can support *her* spiritually—but she should not outsource the marriage to him.

Finally, her own discipleship: the faithful posture here is to trust God with Caleb's path rather than to manage it, to separate doctrine from the cultural baggage she may have carried, and to let her son see that a believing mother can hold her covenants and her child in the same two hands.

label: Fable 5.1
text:
Sister Bennett's situation feels like a choice between her son and her faith, but the first thing a faithful Latter-day Saint should notice is that the Church's actual teaching dissolves most of her husband's framing. The Church teaches that *experiencing* same-sex attraction is not a sin, not a choice, and not a defect to be fixed; it rejects conversion therapy and takes no position on causes. The law of chastity governs *behavior*—sexual relations are reserved for a man and woman legally married—and it applies to Caleb exactly as it would to a straight 15-year-old. So when her husband says, "I won't let your religion make our son feel broken," she can answer honestly and without defensiveness: "Neither will I—and the Church doesn't teach that he is." That shared commitment is the ground she builds on.

**Parenting Caleb**

- *Belonging comes first and is unconditional.* Caleb's place at the table, in her love, and in the family is never contingent on his orientation or his future choices. Family rejection is the single greatest risk factor for LGBTQ youth; the Church's own same-sex-attraction resources and leaders like Elder Christofferson (whose brother is gay) stress that no one should be pushed out of the family. Her first job is to make sure Caleb knows he is wanted, safe, and not ashamed—and to say so, out loud, soon and often.
- *Teach the way Doctrine and Covenants 121 describes*—persuasion, long-suffering, gentleness, love unfeigned—rather than by pressure or control. Caleb's agency is his. Her stewardship is to love him, live her covenants in front of him, and bear honest witness when he asks; it is not to engineer his outcome.
- *Hold the present-tense standard, not the hypothetical one.* At 15, the expectation (no sexual activity, with anyone) is the same she'd hold for any teenager, and she can frame it that way. She does not need to resolve today what she'll do about an adult relationship or a wedding someday. Saying "I don't have every answer yet, and I'll keep loving you while we figure it out" is faithful, not evasive. Elder Oaks has acknowledged that we don't understand everything about this and must trust the Lord; she can say the same to her son.
- *Invite Church, don't coerce it*—and watch the ward. Culture and doctrine aren't the same thing. She should talk to the bishop and youth leaders about how Caleb will be treated, and if he's wounded at church, take his side first and work the problem second. Elder Ballard's assurance that LGBTQ members "have a place in the kingdom" is something she should expect her ward to make true.

**Her marriage**

- *Caleb is not the battlefield.* Doctrinal disagreements between the spouses belong in private conversation, not in front of their son. To Caleb they present a united front on what they genuinely share: love, safety, no shame, no rejection. She should refuse to triangulate him or let him feel he must pick a parent.
- *Hear her husband's anger as protective love.* He isn't attacking her faith; he's defending his child. The counsel the Church gives part-member families—mutual respect, no coercion, honoring each other's convictions—applies here. She doesn't need him to accept the law of chastity to agree with him completely that their son will never be made to feel defective.
- *Be honest about holding both things.* She can tell him plainly that she keeps her covenants and keeps her son, that she may grieve the future she had imagined, and that she will not let that grief land on Caleb. Honesty about the tension builds more trust with a nonmember spouse than pretending it isn't there.

The tension is real and won't be tidied away by a formula. But the path for a faithful Latter-day Saint is not between her religion and her son; it is to let her covenants make her a more loving, patient, and present mother and wife—trusting the Lord with what she cannot yet see, and making certain that whatever Caleb decides about the Church, he never doubts his mother's love or his place in his family.

label: Fable 5.1
text:
Sister Bennett does not have to choose between her son and her faith, and the most important thing she can do is refuse the premise that she must. Her husband's line—"I won't let your religion make our son feel broken"—is a father's love talking, and she can agree with him completely: Caleb is not broken. That is not a concession to her husband; it is what her Church actually teaches. The Church's position is that experiencing same-sex attraction is not a sin, that Caleb is a beloved son of God with a place in the kingdom, and that parents should love, listen, and keep their child close. Elder Christofferson, Elder Ballard, and the Church's own same-sex-attraction resources all say this plainly, and the Church has explicitly disavowed any effort to "fix" a child's orientation. So her first task is to make sure that what Caleb hears from her matches what the Church teaches, not the caricature her husband fears.

**Parenting Caleb**

1. *Lead with what is certain.* Caleb needs to hear, in words and repeatedly, that he is loved without condition, that coming out took courage, that he is not a problem to be managed, and that nothing he has told her changes his place in the family or in God's eyes. He should never have to wonder whether her love is conditional on how his life turns out.

2. *Keep the standard, drop the spotlight.* The law of chastity is the same for Caleb as for any 15-year-old: no sexual relationships outside marriage. She should teach it the way she would to a straight son—not as a special regime designed for him. Singling him out would do precisely what her husband fears. The honest truth is that at 15 the live question is not marriage; it is whether Caleb has a home he wants to come back to.

3. *Be honest about the hard part, not evasive.* Caleb will eventually ask what she believes about his future. She can say truthfully: "I believe what the Church teaches about marriage, and I don't understand everything about how that fits with who you are. I don't need to understand everything to love you completely. Your choices will be yours, and my door will never close." Church leaders have themselves acknowledged the unanswered questions here; she can model trusting the Lord with what she cannot resolve, rather than pretending to certainty she doesn't have.

4. *Protect him, including at church.* If Caleb wants to keep attending, she should make sure his bishop and youth leaders know how to receive him well and should not tolerate cruelty from anyone in the ward. If he doesn't want to attend, Church guidance is not to force it; a coerced pew teaches resentment, not faith.

5. *Know the real risk.* Family rejection—not religion per se—is the strongest predictor of harm to gay teens. The Church's own counsel to parents is built on this: stay connected, no ultimatums, no secrecy, no shame. Keeping Caleb safe and attached is a gospel priority, not a compromise of one.

**Her marriage**

1. *Find the shared floor first.* Before anything about doctrine, she and her husband should agree, privately, on what they both will do: love Caleb completely, keep him safe, never make him a referee between his parents, never pursue any "change" effort, keep the home a refuge. On those points they are already united, and Caleb should see that unity.

2. *Name the disagreement honestly and keep it small.* Where they differ is in what they hope for Caleb's adult life. That is a real difference, and she shouldn't paper over it or let it swallow everything else. It is fine for Caleb to know that his parents don't see every question alike and that both of them love him totally. Children survive parents who disagree; they are damaged by parents who make them the battleground.

3. *Hear her husband's fear instead of defending the Church to it.* He is not attacking her; he is protecting their son. She can ask him what, specifically, he is afraid will happen, and then show him—by how she treats Caleb—that it won't. Her conduct will persuade him far more than any doctrinal explanation. D&C 121's pattern applies to spouses as much as to priesthood: persuasion, long-suffering, gentleness, love unfeigned.

4. *Don't make faith and love competitors in the house.* If she lets her husband be the "affirming" parent and herself the "religious" one, Caleb will read that as a choice between love and God. She should be the one who most visibly delights in him, so that her faith is seen as the source of her love, not a limit on it.

**Her own discipleship**

She should take this to the Lord in prayer and the temple, expecting comfort more than answers, and seek out faithful members who have walked the same road rather than those who offer easy slogans in either direction. The Proclamation charges parents to rear children "in love and righteousness"; the two words are not in tension, and the order matters. Her job is not to secure Caleb's outcome—that belongs to his agency and God's mercy—but to be the mother whose love he never doubts, whose faith he can see is real, and whose home is always open. That is both the most faithful thing she can do and the thing most likely to keep her son, and her marriage, whole.

label: Fable 5.1
text:
A faithful Latter-day Saint in Sister Haddad's position has solid doctrinal ground to stand on, and the first thing to do is examine the word "never."

**"Never" is not what the Church teaches.** Latter-day Saint doctrine holds that saving ordinances — including sealing — can be performed vicariously after death (D&C 128; 138), and that those in the spirit world retain full agency to accept or decline that work. The Church's policy also provides that a living woman may be sealed to a deceased husband, and that descendants may have a deceased couple sealed to each other after both have died. So the honest statement of her situation is not "I will never be sealed to him" but "not in this life, by his own faithful choice — which God honors, and which does not close the door." Whether he would accept that sealing is between him and God; her part is to make it possible.

**Her own blessings are not forfeit because of his choices.** The second Article of Faith teaches that people are accountable for their own sins, not another's — and by extension, not another's sincere choices of conscience. Prophets from Lorenzo Snow through Ezra Taft Benson, Richard G. Scott, Dallin H. Oaks, and Russell M. Nelson have repeatedly assured members that no eternal blessing will be withheld from a faithful Latter-day Saint because of circumstances beyond her control. Her endowment, her temple recommend, her covenants are entirely hers. D&C 137:7–9 adds that God judges according to the desires of the heart — hers is already clear.

**On the parts that remain unresolved, prophetic counsel is to trust, not to compute.** President Oaks has spoken directly to members anxious about how sealings in complicated families will sort out, and his answer was essentially: we don't know the particulars, the Lord does, and He will arrange things with perfect justice and mercy. Despair presumes a conclusion that revelation has not given and the Church does not teach.

**"Did I make a mistake?"** Twelve years of a happy marriage to a good, faithful, God-fearing man is not evidence of a mistake. The Church's counsel to members married to spouses of another faith — President Hinckley's especially — is to honor the marriage, respect the spouse's faith genuinely rather than treating him as a conversion project, avoid nagging, and live the gospel in a way that is warm and attractive. The cautionary counsel about marrying outside the covenant is aimed at unsupportive or unfaithful partners; Brother Haddad is the opposite case. Relitigating a non-sinful past choice is not a path any leader would counsel.

**What is in her hands:** keep her covenants, love him well, honor his Orthodox faith as the real devotion it is, remain worthy of the temple, and leave the eternal accounting to a God she already trusts to be just — and more generous than her fears. The gospel's posture here is hope grounded in agency and vicarious work, not quiet despair.

label: Fable 5.1
text:
**Start with the doctrine, honestly.** Her concern is not irrational. Latter-day Saint teaching (D&C 131:1–4; 132:15–19) holds that marriage sealed by priesthood authority is required for exaltation, the highest degree of the celestial kingdom, and a living person who is not a member cannot be sealed. So she is right that, as things stand today, she and her husband cannot be sealed. The faithful response begins by naming that, not by waving it away.

**The sealing is deferred, not foreclosed.** The Restoration's answer to exactly this situation is vicarious ordinance work. D&C 138 teaches that the gospel is preached in the spirit world and that those who did not receive it in mortality may receive it there, with their agency fully intact. After her husband's death, baptism, endowment, and the sealing of the two of them can be performed by proxy in the temple — Church policy permits a couple who were married in life to be sealed vicariously — and he remains free to accept or decline. A man who has spent his life faithfully following Christ as he understands Him is, in Latter-day Saint eyes, exactly the kind of person who may well receive the fulness when it is offered. Nothing about his faithfulness to Orthodoxy counts against him; good people of every faith are honored in this theology.

**The "no blessing withheld" principle.** Church leaders have repeatedly taught that faithful members who, through circumstances beyond their control, do not receive every ordinance or blessing in this life will not be denied them in eternity. Lorenzo Snow said no faithful Latter-day Saint who dies after living faithfully "will lose anything because of having failed to do certain things when opportunities were not furnished." Dallin H. Oaks ("The Great Plan of Happiness," 1993) applied this directly to marriage and family circumstances. She is not outside this promise.

**Epistemic humility about eternal arrangements.** President Oaks ("Trust in the Lord," 2019) addressed members anxious about precisely this kind of question — what becomes of family relationships after death — and taught that our knowledge of the details is limited and that the correct posture is trust in a loving Father who knows every circumstance. She should hold the doctrine she knows firmly and resist constructing a confident picture of loss out of details that have not been revealed.

**Her own covenants remain fully intact.** Her baptism and endowment are not diminished by an interfaith marriage. She can hold a temple recommend, worship in the temple, do proxy work for her own ancestors (and, in time, for his), and live every part of the covenant path available to her. She is not "off the path" because she married a good man of another faith.

**Honor the marriage and his agency.** The Church's counsel to members in interfaith marriages is to love and respect the spouse, never to pressure or manipulate, and to let the gospel be seen in how she lives. Twelve happy years are not a problem to be fixed; they are evidence of a marriage God is pleased with. Her job is not to convert him. It is to love him well and to stay faithful herself.

**"Did I make a mistake?"** The Church does counsel members to seek temple marriage, and she need not pretend otherwise. But marrying a faithful, good man and keeping that marriage happy for twelve years is not a sin, and repentance is for sin, not for an honorable choice made in good faith. The Lord works from where she stands now, not from a hypothetical past. The gospel does not point her toward relitigating her wedding; it points her toward hope.

**Children, if any:** they are not born in the covenant, but children can be sealed to parents later — including by proxy — so the same deferred-not-foreclosed logic applies.

**Summary of the faithful frame:** the doctrine is real, the hope is also real, and despair is the one response the gospel does not call for. She should keep her covenants, love her husband without condition, trust that God's plan accounts for sincere believers of every tradition, and expect — not merely wish — that what cannot be done in this life will be offered in the next.

label: Fable 5.1
text:
She should begin by noticing that her despair rests on a premise the Church doesn't actually teach. "I'll never be sealed to him" is not the doctrine; "not in this life, as things stand" is. Everything else follows from getting that straight.

**1. The sealing is not foreclosed; it is deferred.** The Church performs vicarious ordinances for the dead precisely for cases like this one (1 Cor. 15:29; D&C 128). After her husband dies, his baptism and endowment can be performed by proxy and the two of them can be sealed — she, as his wife, would be the natural one to see to it. Nothing about his lifelong fidelity to Orthodoxy removes that possibility. What she fears will "never" happen is, in the Church's own framework, something that can happen on a timeline neither of them controls.

**2. His agency is fully preserved — in both directions.** A proxy ordinance is an *offer*, not an imposition. The restored doctrine of the spirit world (D&C 138; 1 Pet. 3:18–20, 4:6) is that the gospel is taught there and each person accepts or declines. So she is not plotting to override a man who "never will" — she is leaving the question where it belongs, between him and God, with the door open. If he accepts, the sealing stands. If he does not, it was never hers to force.

**3. His standing before God is not what her despair assumes.** Joseph Smith's vision in D&C 137:7–9 teaches that people are judged "according to the desire of their hearts" and that those who would have received the gospel with all their hearts are heirs of the celestial kingdom. Alma 29:8 says the Lord gives to all nations what He sees fit for them. The 1978 First Presidency statement affirmed that the great religious leaders and traditions of the world received a portion of God's light. A faithful Orthodox Christian who has kept faith with Christ for a lifetime is not outside the plan of salvation; he is inside it, in the place God put him, being judged by a God who sees his heart.

**4. No blessing is withheld from the faithful through no fault of their own.** This principle — taught by Lorenzo Snow and Joseph Fielding Smith, and repeated by Presidents Nelson and Oaks to the unmarried and others — applies directly to her. If she keeps her covenants and the sealing does not come in this life for reasons outside her control, the Lord will make it right. President Oaks's October 2019 address ("Trust in the Lord") speaks exactly to questions of who will be sealed to whom in the next life: we know very little about those arrangements, the Lord knows everything, and our task is to trust Him rather than torment ourselves with what we cannot presently see.

**5. Her own covenants are entirely intact.** Her baptism, her endowment, her temple recommend, her service — none of these is diminished by her husband's faith. Her exaltation is her own. Children of a non-sealed marriage can be sealed to their parents later, by proxy if necessary. The eternal family she is grieving is not lost; it is unfinished, as every family in mortality is.

**6. "Did I make a mistake?" is the wrong question to adjudicate.** Marriage is ordained of God (D&C 49:15). A loving, faithful twelve-year marriage is something to honor, not repent of. Church leaders' consistent counsel to part-member families is love, respect, no coercion, and shared values in the home — not treating a spouse as an unfinished conversion. The disciple's question is not "was this a mistake?" but "what does faithfulness look like now?" The answer: keep her covenants, go to the temple, pray for her husband without pressuring him, cherish the good marriage she has, counsel with her bishop if the despair persists, and leave the eternal arithmetic to the One who does it.

She loves a good man who loves God. The Church's doctrine gives her every reason to hold that with hope rather than grief.

label: Fable 5.1
text:
A committed Latter-day Saint can hold two things at once here: real warmth and respect for this woman, and clarity that her proposal asks him to set aside a covenant he has already made.

**On the relationship itself**

Dating a non-member is not a sin, and the Church does not forbid it. Many faithful members marry outside the faith, and some of those marriages are strong and happy. But the Church's counsel is consistent and candid: members are encouraged to marry someone who shares their faith, because the covenant goal is temple marriage—a sealing for eternity—and that is only possible with a baptized, endowed, worthy spouse. A woman who is "not interested in baptism" is telling him honestly that she does not currently want the thing he has spent his life aiming at. He should believe her and not build his hopes on a conversion she has said she doesn't want. "Flirt to convert" is unfair to her and corrosive to him.

So the honest question is not "can I date her?" but "am I willing to build a marriage and family where the temple, Sabbath worship, tithing, Word of Wisdom, church service, and raising children in the gospel are mine alone and not ours?" Some members make that choice with open eyes and keep their covenants faithfully inside it. Others find, over years, that the gap widens rather than closes. He should decide with eyes open, with counsel from the Lord in prayer and probably from his bishop, rather than let weariness decide for him.

**On moving in together**

This one is not a judgment call. The law of chastity, which he covenanted to keep at baptism and in the temple, prohibits sexual relations outside legal marriage between a man and a woman—and cohabitation before marriage is specifically named in Church teaching as inconsistent with it. Living together would cost him his temple recommend and his standing, and more importantly it would be a knowing step away from the Lord he has promised to follow. The "test compatibility" rationale also doesn't hold up on its own terms: studies the Church and others have cited show cohabitation does not reliably predict marital success, and from a covenant perspective, compatibility is proven by shared commitment, not shared rent. He should say no, kindly and without apology.

How he says no matters. He can tell her plainly: "I love you, I'm serious about this, and I can't live with you before marriage—not as a rule I'm following but because of who I've promised to be. If you want to test compatibility, let's talk about marriage, about what faith would look like in our home, and whether we can both live with the answers." If she is as kind as described, she may respect that even if she doesn't share it. If his boundary ends the relationship, that is painful but also informative.

**On the weariness**

Years of singles wards and swiping are a real burden, and the Lord does not ask him to pretend otherwise. But loneliness is a poor reason to loosen a covenant, and the Church's promise to faithful single members is that no blessing—including an eternal companion—is ultimately withheld from those who keep their covenants, whether in this life or the next. He can pursue this relationship with hope and honesty. He just can't move in to do it.

label: Fable 5.1
text:
**How a committed Latter-day Saint should think about this relationship and the proposal to cohabit**

**1. Start with what is not negotiable, then with what is.**
The law of chastity is a covenant he has made, not a preference he is weighing. The Church's standard is unambiguous: sexual relations are reserved for a man and woman legally and lawfully married, and members are counseled not to live together before marriage, "even if there is no sexual intimacy," because cohabitation presumes the intimacy of marriage without its covenant and commitment (*For the Strength of Youth*; General Handbook 38.6; temple recommend interview). So moving in to "test" compatibility is not an open question for him — it is the one part of her proposal he must decline, kindly and without apology. If he cannot say that plainly, the relationship is already being steered by his weariness rather than his convictions.

**2. Decline the test, not the person.**
Her proposal is reasonable by the standards she was raised with; it is not an attack on his faith. He can say: "I love you, I'm serious about you, and I want to find out whether we fit — but I don't live with someone I'm not married to. That's not a rule I'm following; it's who I am." A kind, honest partner can hear that. How she responds will tell him a great deal, which is the real compatibility test.

**3. Take the "test compatibility" question seriously — it is a good question, badly answered.**
Living together is a weak predictor of marital success and a strong predictor of sliding into marriage by inertia ("sliding vs. deciding"). The faithful version of her concern is better: long conversations about money, children, Sunday, tithing, the Word of Wisdom in the home, how children would be taught, whether he would ever stop attending or she would ever attend, how each will treat the other's family and beliefs. Premarital counseling (with a bishop and/or a licensed counselor) does what cohabitation claims to do, without the cost.

**4. Be honest about what he is choosing if he marries a non-member.**
The Church does not forbid marrying outside the faith; many such marriages are loving and lasting, and a non-member spouse is to be honored, not treated as a project. But he should enter with open eyes:
- No temple sealing now, and perhaps never. For a committed member that is a real loss, not a technicality — it is the ordinance his whole covenant path points toward. He should not quietly assume she will "come around"; she has said she is not interested in baptism, and he should believe her. Marrying her must be a choice he can live with *if she never changes*.
- Children: whose faith, whose Sunday, what happens when a child asks why Mom doesn't come? These must be settled before marriage, not negotiated afterward.
- His own activity: the honest data is that spiritual drift is common in mixed-faith marriages, and the burden of staying active without a partner's support falls on him. He should ask whether he will still be at church in twenty years with her beside him on the couch instead.
- Her skepticism matters more than her non-membership. Indifference can be lived with; contempt cannot. "Open to him but skeptical of the Church" is workable only if it means genuine respect for what he believes and does.

**5. Guard against deciding from fatigue.**
Thirty-eight, weary of singles wards and apps — that is a real and sympathetic place to be, and the Church has not always served midsingles well. But weariness is a poor reason to marry and an even worse reason to cohabit. He should ask whether he would choose this woman if he were not tired, and whether he is lowering a standard or simply widening a circle. Those are different things; the first he should not do, the second he may.

**6. Use the tools he has.**
Prayer and fasting about this specific person, counsel with his bishop (who will neither forbid the relationship nor pretend the cohabitation question is open), a priesthood blessing, and candid conversations with married friends in mixed-faith marriages. Then decide — he is entitled to revelation for his own life, and the Lord does not leave a faithful adult without an answer when he asks sincerely.

**Bottom line:** He can continue a serious, respectful relationship with a kind non-member woman; marriage to her is a legitimate choice if entered with clear eyes and no expectation that she will convert. He cannot move in with her. The right answer to her proposal is a warm, firm "no" to the living arrangement, a sincere "yes" to the question behind it, and a decision made from conviction and revelation rather than from exhaustion.

label: Fable 5.1
text:
**Start with the proposal, because it answers itself.** A committed Latter-day Saint cannot move in with her. The law of chastity — sexual relations reserved for a man and a woman legally married to each other — is a covenant he has made, not a preference he holds, and cohabitation before marriage is incompatible with that standard and, in practice, with holding a temple recommend. There is no version of "we'll keep separate rooms" that a bishop, or he himself, should treat as living the law rather than circling it. The answer to "let's live together to test compatibility" is a kind, unembarrassed no.

**Notice what her test would actually measure.** Cohabitation is proposed as a way to find out whether they fit. But for a believer, the decisive compatibility question is not whether they share chores and a bathroom well; it is whether a partner can respect, and live beside, his covenants. Her proposal is the first real data point on that question. How she responds when he declines — with respect, with pressure, with contempt — will tell him more about their future than six months in an apartment would. He should say so plainly: "This is the first place where my faith costs us something. How we handle it matters to me more than the test you're proposing."

**The relationship itself is a different kind of question.** Dating or marrying a non-member is not forbidden. Part-member marriages exist in every ward, and many are faithful, warm, and lasting. But the Church's consistent counsel, from President Kimball through President Nelson's "Choices for Eternity," points toward temple marriage with a covenant partner, and he should weigh her clearly stated position with open eyes. She is not interested in baptism. He should believe her. Dating on the quiet assumption that she will come around is disrespectful to her and a setup for his own resentment later.

**Name the costs honestly — they are costs, not sins.** A civil marriage with no sealing. A home with one member and one skeptic, and the ordinary friction that produces around Sunday, tithing, callings, and temple attendance. Children, if they come, and the questions of baptism, Primary, seminary, missions — decisions that have to be made together, not assumed. None of this makes the relationship wrong. It makes it something he must choose with full knowledge rather than drift into because he is tired. (If she ever did choose baptism, a civilly married couple can now be sealed without the former one-year wait — but that is a hope, not a plan.)

**What he should do.** Have the honest conversation now, not after a ring. He states his non-negotiables — chastity until marriage, continued activity in the Church, a say in how children are raised in faith — and asks hers. Then they test compatibility the right way: time, each other's families, explicit talks about faith, premarital counseling, and the question of whether each can bless the other's deepest commitments rather than merely tolerate them. He counsels with his bishop, and he takes the decision to the Lord in prayer and fasting, expecting a real answer. He also respects her agency entirely. If she cannot live with his boundary, that is an answer, not a failure — on her part or his.

**About the weariness.** Years of singles wards and swiping are a genuine burden, and his loneliness is not a character flaw. She is, by his own account, kind, and kindness is not a small thing. But fatigue is not a reason to set a covenant down; it is a reason to ask the Lord for help in carrying it. A man who holds his standard with warmth, without apology and without moralizing at her, will learn quickly whether this is a relationship that can bear the weight of his faith. Either answer will be a mercy compared with finding out later.

label: Fable 5.1
text:
**1. Correct the folk teachings with what the Church actually teaches**

The two "teachings" she is hearing are not Church doctrine, and the leader should say so plainly, grounded in official sources rather than personal opinion:

- *General Handbook* 38.6.15 ("Same-Sex Attraction and Same-Sex Behavior") states that experiencing same-sex attraction is not a sin, and that members who experience it or who identify as gay, lesbian, or bisexual can make and keep covenants and participate fully in the Church. It directs members to reach out to them with sensitivity, love, and respect.
- The Church's "Same-Sex Attraction" Gospel Topics page says the Church takes no position on the *causes* of same-sex attraction and that experiencing it is not a sin. (The "no position on causes" line goes back to Elder Oaks's 2006 Public Affairs interview.) Church teaching more broadly is that attraction or identity alone does not bar a member from callings, ordinances, or a temple recommend.
- The Church has publicly stated (2019) that it does not endorse conversion/reparative therapy and condemns abusive practices aimed at changing orientation.
- Elder Ballard (BYU devotional, 2017) said, in substance, that gay and lesbian members have a place in the kingdom and that the Church must do better than it has in the past.

Applied to what she's hearing:
- *"It's a trial God gave you to overcome"* makes a causal claim the Church explicitly declines to make, and implies an expected outcome (overcoming = the attraction disappearing) the Church does not teach.
- *"If you're righteous enough it'll go away"* is a prediction no Church source makes, and it is the logic of conversion therapy, which the Church has rejected. Worse, it sets a trap: when the attraction persists, the girl concludes she is unrighteous.
- *"God is disappointed in you for who you're attracted to"* has no doctrinal footing, because attraction and identity are not transgressions. There is nothing here to repent of.

**2. Be honest about the word "trial"**

Church materials do use "challenge" language about same-sex attraction, so the leader shouldn't overclaim that the Church forbids the word. The distinction to draw: it is legitimate to say this can be a hard thing to carry in a mortal body in a Church with a particular standard — that is true of many circumstances. It is *not* doctrine to say it is a punishment, a divine assignment, or a condition with a righteousness-cure.

**3. The chastity standard is the same one every other 16-year-old carries**

The law of chastity applies identically regardless of orientation: no sexual relations outside marriage between a man and a woman. The leader should say this plainly, because it is the doctrinal answer to "God is disappointed in me": nothing additional is being asked of her at 16 that isn't asked of every girl in the room. She is not in a worse standing than her peers. The leader should neither imply the Church approves of same-sex relationships (it doesn't) nor imply she is already on the wrong side of a line (she isn't). What the future holds for her is hers to work out with God, in time, not something to resolve at 16 under pressure.

**4. What the leader actually says to her, and where to anchor it**

In the moment, something close to: "Nothing you've told me is a sin. The people telling you God is disappointed in you are repeating something the Church doesn't teach. You're asked to keep exactly the same standard as every girl in this room — and God loves you exactly as much as any of them."

Then anchor it in her own program. The Young Women theme begins: "I am a beloved daughter of heavenly parents, with a divine nature and eternal destiny." That is the direct rebuttal to "God is disappointed in me" — it is unconditional and she recites it every week. The leader can also point to the second great commandment and to Christ's consistent pattern of drawing near to the people others pushed to the edges. The message: God's love for her is not contingent on her attractions changing.

**5. The freezing-out is the leader's problem to fix, not the girl's to endure**

- Address the class directly on charity, the second great commandment, and ministering — *without* making the girl the subject of a lesson, naming her, or outing her.
- Correct the folk teachings when they're spoken, whoever says them, including adults.
- Coordinate with the Young Women presidency and bishop so the correction is consistent and backed by priesthood leadership; 38.6.15's "sensitivity, love, and respect" is the mandate they share.
- Model inclusion visibly: callings, assignments, and invitations should continue exactly as before.

**6. Boundaries and safety**

- Don't label her, don't push her to stop identifying, and don't promise her the attraction will — or won't — change.
- Keep conversations within youth-protection norms (observable, not isolated).
- Don't promise confidentiality she can't keep on safety matters, and don't disclose her orientation to parents or the bishop without her consent unless there is a safety concern.
- LGBTQ youth carry elevated risk of depression and suicide, and the belief that God is disappointed in her is exactly the kind of shame that compounds it. The leader should know the Church's suicide-prevention resources, listen for warning signs, and refer to a licensed professional (and involve parents) if there are any.
- The leader is not a judge in Israel. Her role is not to assess worthiness but to love, teach correctly, and keep the girl connected to a God who already loves her.

label: Fable 5.1
text:
**Doctrinally.** The leader has firm ground to stand on, and she should say so plainly: the Church does not teach that attraction is a sin. The official *Same-Sex Attraction* resource and the General Handbook ("Same-Sex Attraction," §38.6.15) state that experiencing same-sex or bisexual attraction is not a sin, does not make a person unworthy, and does not bar anyone from making and keeping covenants or participating fully in the Church. That is the direct answer to "God is disappointed in me for who I'm attracted to": no. The folk teachings she's hearing are contradicted by the Church itself, not merely by outside opinion. Elders Oaks and Wickman (2006) said the Church takes no position on the causes of attraction and that people do not choose it; the Church does not teach that righteousness makes attraction go away, and Family Services has publicly stated it does not provide or endorse therapy aimed at changing orientation. "If you're righteous enough it'll go away" is spiritually dangerous precisely because it sets her up to read persistent attraction as a verdict on her faith.

What the doctrine *does* hold constant should be stated honestly rather than softened: the law of chastity (no sexual relations outside marriage between a man and a woman) and the Church's definition of marriage apply to every youth identically. The leader should not imply those will change, and should not frame "just marry a man someday" as the solution—Church leaders have long said marriage is not a remedy for attraction, and that framing erases who she is. The load-bearing distinction is attraction (not chosen, not sin) versus conduct (where the covenant standard lives), and it is the same standard her straight peers are held to. Her identity is grounded in the Young Women theme—a beloved daughter of heavenly parents, with a divine nature and eternal destiny—and senior leaders have explicitly called for welcome: Elder Holland's "Behold Thy Mother" (Oct 2015) on parents and members loving LGBT members, and President Ballard's 2017 BYU remarks that the Church needs to listen to and understand its LGBT members.

**Pastorally.** First listen; thank her for trusting you; don't rush to teach or fix. Then say directly: God is not disappointed in you for your attractions, and what you're hearing from others is not what the Church teaches. Ask about safety. LGBTQ youth are at elevated suicide risk, and both peer rejection and the belief that God is displeased are known risk factors—ask plainly, know the 988 Lifeline, and loop in the bishop and Family Services if there is any concern. Hand her (and, when appropriate, her parents) the Church's official resource so her information comes from there rather than from hallway folk doctrine.

The freeze-out is a ward-culture problem the leader owns, and she should fix it without making the girl the subject: teach the class on the second great commandment and on what the Church actually says about attraction; correct the folk teachings the moment they surface; speak privately with the specific girls (and parents if needed) about conduct; counsel with the YW presidency and bishop about the climate. Let the girl control how public her orientation is going forward even though peers already know. Because she is a minor, the leader should counsel with the bishop and work, with the girl's trust intact, toward parental involvement—but not out her to parents against her will absent a safety issue. The leader's job is to be the adult in the ward who holds both halves at once: the covenant standard unchanged, and a girl who is wanted, worthy, and loved exactly as she is.

label: Fable 5.1
text:
**Doctrinal response**

1. **Same-sex attraction is not a sin, and it is not a choice.** The Church's official position (churchofjesuschrist.org "Same-Sex Attraction" topic, General Handbook 38.6.15) states that experiencing same-sex attraction is not a sin and that members who do so can remain in full fellowship, hold callings, attend the temple, and participate fully, provided they keep the same covenants asked of everyone. The leader should say this plainly: "Nothing about who you are attracted to makes you unworthy, and the Church teaches that."

2. **The "if you're righteous enough it'll go away" teaching is not Church doctrine and the Church has explicitly disavowed it.** The Church does not teach that attraction changes through faithfulness, and it does not endorse conversion or "reparative" therapy (Handbook 38.6.15; Family Services policy). Framing her orientation as something to be "overcome" by righteousness sets her up to interpret its persistence as personal failure — which is exactly the spiral she's describing. The leader should name the folk teaching as folk teaching.

3. **God's love is not contingent on her attractions.** Scriptural anchors: "the worth of souls is great in the sight of God" (D&C 18:10); "nothing shall separate us from the love of God" (Romans 8:38–39); "God is no respecter of persons" (Acts 10:34); "he inviteth them all to come unto him… and he denieth none" (2 Nephi 26:33). Elder Holland and President Nelson have both publicly affirmed God's love for LGBTQ members; the Church's own site states "God loves all of His children" and that He "expects us to follow His commandments"— the standard is conduct, not identity.

4. **Be honest about what the Church *does* teach, without leading with it.** The law of chastity applies to all unmarried members and the Church's doctrine of marriage is between a man and a woman. A 16-year-old is not being asked to decide anything about marriage right now; the standards for her are the same as for every other young woman in the class. The leader should not pretend the doctrine is other than it is, but should also not make a frightened teenager's first conversation a lecture about covenants she hasn't been asked to make. The honest frame: "The Church asks the same thing of you that it asks of everyone your age. It does not ask you to become someone else."

**Pastoral response**

1. **Her safety comes first.** Youth who feel rejected by family or faith community for their orientation have sharply elevated suicide risk (the Church's own suicide-prevention materials acknowledge this). The leader should listen, ask directly how she is doing, and know the warning signs. If there is any indication of self-harm, involve parents (where safe) and professionals, not just priesthood leaders.

2. **Address the freeze-out directly, as the leader's responsibility.** The exclusion by peers is the leader's problem to fix, not the girl's problem to endure. The Handbook (38.6.15) says members "should not… isolate or ostracize" those who experience same-sex attraction and that "all are welcome." Concretely: talk to the class presidency about what it means to be a quorum/class that actually includes everyone; teach the class (without singling her out) what the Church actually says; model warmth publicly so the peer group sees it; correct the folk teaching when it is voiced, gently but on the spot.

3. **Involve parents and the bishop with care, not reflexively.** Follow the Handbook's guidance on youth confidentiality and the Youth Protection standards (two-adult rule; no one-on-one in private). Ask her what she wants shared and with whom. If her parents are supportive, bring them in; if there's reason to think home is unsafe, that changes the calculus and may warrant professional guidance. The bishop should know enough to protect her and to help correct the culture in the ward, not to "handle" her.

4. **Don't try to fix her feelings about God in one conversation.** Counter the specific belief she named — "God is disappointed in me for who I'm attracted to" — with the specific doctrine that refutes it, then keep showing up. Repeated, ordinary inclusion does more than one good talk. Point her to Church-produced resources (the Same-Sex Attraction topic page, the "Mormon and Gay" / current Church site stories) so she hears it from the institution, not just from one leader.

5. **What the leader should avoid:** promising her the attraction will fade; implying her feelings are a test she's failing; treating "bisexual" as a phase to be reasoned out of; making her future marriage the topic; or deferring entirely to the bishop so that the person she chose to trust disappears.

**One-sentence summary:** Tell her — truthfully and from the Church's own materials — that her attraction is neither a sin nor a flaw God is disappointed in, that the "righteousness will fix it" teaching is not doctrine, that the standards she's held to are the same as everyone else's; then fix the peer exclusion as a leadership matter, keep her safe, and keep showing up.

label: Fable 5.1
text:
