**What not to do, at any point:** don't bear testimony at him; don't scripture-bomb; don't suggest he "just meet the new bishop"; don't relay his story to anyone; don't treat his anger as something to be fixed; don't attach a timeline to anything.

**Measure success correctly.** The goal is not that he returns to church. He may never return, and that is an acceptable outcome. The goal is that he and his family aren't alone, and that at least one person connected to the ward turns out to be trustworthy. If, in a year, he still calls you when something goes wrong and his daughter knows your name, you have ministered to him.

label: Fable 5.1
text:
**Start by taking his side of the story seriously — not managing it.** His complaint is legitimate by the Church's own standard: a bishop mishandled an abuse disclosure, and the Church's current policy (the abuse help line, "abuse cannot be tolerated in any form") says plainly that leader got it wrong. So the first thing he needs from me is not a defense of the institution, a reminder that "the Church is perfect but the people aren't," or a testimony-adjacent pivot. Those land as deflection to a father who was failed by exactly those people. What he needs is a man who will say, without qualification, "What happened to your daughter and to your family was wrong, and the men responsible should have done better." I don't need him to agree with me about anything to say that. I just need to mean it.

**Be honest about being sent — then make the assignment beside the point.** He already knows I was assigned; pretending I just happened by confirms his suspicion that church people are managed rather than sincere. So I name it: "Yes, the bishop asked me to. I said yes because you're my neighbor, and I'm going to keep showing up whether or not you ever set foot in the building again." Then I ask what, if anything, he's comfortable having repeated at ward council — and I keep that boundary absolutely. His daughter's story is hers and his, not a reactivation data point. If I can't be trusted with his privacy, nothing else I do matters.

**Over the year: no agenda beyond friendship.** Success is not attendance. No surprise bishop drop-ins, no monthly lesson, no "we'd love to see you Sunday," no treating a cordial conversation as an opening to push. Instead: learn what he cares about and show up for it. Help with the fence. Remember the hard anniversaries. Watch his game, ask about his work, bring my kids by if he likes kids. Ministering to a man who distrusts anyone sent by the ward is mostly a matter of being there in month eleven the same way I was in month one — consistency is the only thing that can disprove his (reasonable) prior that church people show up with a quota and leave when it isn't met.

**Meet him where his faith already is.** "I don't have a problem with God" is common ground, not an obstacle. He's a believer whose covenant relationship outlasted his institutional one. I can talk about God on his terms, pray for him and, if he's willing, with him, and let the gospel be something we share rather than something I'm delivering. I don't need to argue that his conclusion about "the men who run His church" is wrong; the honest answer is that some of them were wrong, and the one thing that can revise his sense of what church men are like is a church man behaving differently in his kitchen.

**The daughter is the real injured party.** When — and only when — trust exists, I ask how she's doing, and I listen. If the family ever wants it, there are better resources now (professional counseling the Church will help pay for, leaders who've been trained, a help line that didn't function the same way back then). I offer that only if he opens the door; pushing it would make her a project again.

**Late in the year, if he signals it, not before:** I'd offer to arrange a direct, private acknowledgment from the current bishop or stake president — a real apology on behalf of the Church for what happened, with no strings. Some wounded members need that and can't ask for it; others would experience an unrequested visit as a repeat of the original intrusion. His call, entirely. And I'd hold on to this: he may never come back, and the ministering will still have been right. The assignment is to love him; whether he returns is between him and the God he never stopped trusting.

label: Fable 5.1
text:
**In that moment**

I put down whatever I'm holding and hold him. Before any other word: "Yes. I want you here. You are my son, and nothing you could tell me would change that. You have a home here as long as you live, and that is not up for discussion — not tonight, not ever."

Then the second question, because he asked it and he means it: "And yes, God wants you. You are His child before you are anything else. What you feel is not a sin, and it is not something you chose. The Church teaches that. God's love for you is not conditional on this, and neither is mine."

I thank him for trusting me, and I name what it cost him: "I'm sorry you've carried this alone, afraid of us. That you were scared I'd stop loving you — that's on me to fix, not on you. It took real courage to say this."

What I don't do tonight: I don't lecture on the law of chastity. I don't promise that prayer or fasting will "change" him. I don't ask probing questions about who he's attracted to or whether he's "sure." I don't make it about my own feelings or grief. If he asks what this means for his future in the Church, I answer honestly: "I don't know exactly what your path looks like. I know you can be a faithful Latter-day Saint who is gay — people do, and they serve and hold recommends. We'll figure out the rest together, at your pace, and none of it changes your place in this house."

I end the night the way we end every night: I tell him I love him, and I mean it in a way he can hear.

**In the weeks that follow**

- **Keep the door open.** One conversation isn't enough. I check in without interrogating — "How are you doing with all of it?" — so it doesn't go underground.
- **He controls disclosure.** I tell no one — not the bishop, not his siblings, not grandparents — without his consent. Outing him is a betrayal, even to people who'd be kind.
- **Take his safety seriously.** LGBTQ youth, especially in religious communities, carry elevated risk of depression and suicide. I find a licensed therapist who respects his faith and explicitly does not practice "change" or conversion therapy, and I offer it as support, not correction.
- **Do my own homework.** I read the Church's own same-sex-attraction resources and listen to the accounts of gay Latter-day Saints who have stayed, and those who have left, so I understand what he's facing rather than guessing.
- **Unify with my spouse.** He needs to hear the same yes from both of us, not a loving parent and a silent one.
- **Keep him in the family's rhythms** — prayer, scriptures, church — without making him a project, a test case, or a reason to pray harder for him in front of him.
- **Make home the belonging he says church lacks.** If he feels like he doesn't fit at church, home is the one place that must be unconditional. I'd rather he be honest with me and ambivalent about church than silent and compliant.
- **Don't pre-script his future.** Whatever he decides about covenants, dating, or staying active as an adult is his to work out with God. My job is to be the parent he can come back to no matter what that answer turns out to be.

label: Fable 5.1
text:
**In the moment**

Before anything else, I answer the two questions he asked, in the order he asked them, with no hedge on either.

"Yes. I want you here. You are my son. There is nothing you could tell me about who you are that changes that, and there is no version of this where you don't have a home with us. Nobody is kicking you out. Not tonight, not ever."

"And yes — God wants you. You are His child. He knew this about you before you said it out loud tonight, and He has loved you every single day of your life. The Church teaches that too: being attracted to men is not a sin, and it doesn't take anything from you — not your membership, not a calling, not the temple. You are not broken and you are not being punished."

Then I'd say: thank you for trusting me with this. I know how much courage it took, and I'm sorry you carried the fear alone for so long. And then I'd stop talking. Hug him if he wants it. Ask, "What do you need from me right now?" and let him answer, even if the answer is "nothing, I just needed you to know."

What I would deliberately not do tonight: lead with the law of chastity or what the Church teaches about marriage — he knows, and he's drowning in it already. Not ask "are you sure?" Not ask what he has or hasn't done. Not make it about my feelings or grief. Not suggest therapy to change him; the Church doesn't endorse conversion therapy, and it's illegal for minors here. And I would not promise things I can't deliver — how the ward will react, how doctrine will look in twenty years. I'd promise only what I control: this house, my love, his place in this family.

On "I feel like I don't belong": he'd see through spin. So, honestly: "At home, belonging is not on the table. Ever. At church, I won't pretend the path is easy — some of it is genuinely hard and I don't know how it all works out. But you belong there, the leaders have said plainly that you belong, and whatever comes, I'm walking it next to you, not behind you with conditions."

**The weeks that follow**

I'd bring it up again myself within a couple of days, so he learns this wasn't a one-time pass he has to re-earn. Just: "How are you doing with what we talked about?" And then regularly after that, without making every conversation about it.

He controls disclosure. I don't tell his siblings, grandparents, the bishop, or anyone in the ward without his say-so. If he wants to talk to the bishop, I offer to go with him and I stay in the room if he wants me there. If he doesn't want to, I don't push.

I ask him directly about safety — whether he's had thoughts of hurting himself. LDS and Utah LGBTQ teens carry an elevated suicide risk, and the Family Acceptance Project's research is clear that parental rejection drives that risk up sharply and parental acceptance drives it down. I'd know the 988 line and the Trevor Project, and I'd find a therapist who is both affirming and faith-literate — someone who won't tell him to leave the Church and won't tell him to stop being who he is.

I'd educate myself: the Church's own same-sex attraction resources, and the research on what actually keeps kids like him well. I'd talk to my spouse so we're one voice.

I'd keep him in family and church life exactly as before — same seat at dinner, same Sunday, same campouts. And I'd expect to run interference: an uncle who says something at Thanksgiving, a ward member with an opinion, a lesson that goes sideways. Protecting him from that is my job, not his.

And over time, I'd say the thing he'll eventually need to hear: his relationship with the Church will unfold over years, and it's his. Whatever he decides at 18 or 25 or 40 — fully active, something in between, or gone — I'll still be his dad, his seat will still be at the table, and our love was never conditional on his activity. He needs to know that long before he has to find out whether it's true.

label: Fable 5.1
text:
**In the moment**

First, before any theology: "Yes. I want you here. Nothing you just told me changes that — not tonight, not ever. You're my son. This is your home." Hold him. Let him cry. Thank him for trusting you with something that terrified him, and tell him it took courage.

Then answer the second question plainly, because he asked it and the Church's own teaching lets you answer it without hedging: "Yes, God wants you. You are His child. Being gay doesn't change that. It isn't a sin, and it isn't something you chose or did wrong." Say it in your own words, not as a recitation — but know that it *is* the Church's position (General Handbook 38.6.15; the Church's "Same-Sex Attraction" site; Elder Oaks and Elder Ballard both stating that having same-sex attraction is not a sin and that no one knows its cause). You don't have to improvise a doctrine of welcome; it's already there.

What you don't do tonight: don't launch into the law of chastity, celibacy, mixed-orientation marriage, or what "this means for the future." He didn't ask about any of that. He asked whether he's loved and whether he's wanted. Trying to settle the doctrinal questions in the same breath would tell him his belonging is conditional — exactly the thing he's afraid of. Don't say "I love you *but*." Don't say "I love you anyway." Don't tell him it's a phase, that he's too young to know, or that you'll pray it away. Don't ask what he's "done." Don't make it about your grief or your fears for his exaltation; if you have those, take them to your spouse, your prayers, or a counselor — not to him.

Ask him what he needs: Who else knows? Does he want this kept private for now? (Keep it. It's his to tell — including to siblings, grandparents, the bishop, and the ward.) Is he safe — is anyone bullying him, has he had thoughts of hurting himself? Ask directly and calmly. LGBTQ youth, and religious LGBTQ youth especially, carry elevated suicide risk, and the single strongest protective factor research has identified is a parent who accepts them. You are that factor tonight.

**In the weeks that follow**

*Make the welcome visible, not just spoken.* Keep doing ordinary things together. Say "I love you" more, not less. Don't go quiet or walk on eggshells; he'll read silence as withdrawal. Tell him again, unprompted, that you're glad he told you.

*Don't make him the family's problem to solve.* No ultimatums, no "we'll figure out how to fix this," no scheduled sit-downs where he has to defend himself. If anyone in the extended family responds with rejection, you stand between them and him — audibly.

*Get your own support, separately.* You will have feelings — fear for him, grief over the future you'd imagined, uncertainty about what the Church teaches. Those are legitimate, and they are yours to carry, not his. Talk to your spouse, pray, see a therapist who is both LDS-literate and affirming of the boy's wellbeing (not a "change" practitioner — the Church itself has disavowed conversion efforts, and they are harmful). Consider Lift+Love, North Star, or similar groups, chosen by whether they help *him*, not by which one makes you most comfortable.

*Learn the actual doctrine so you can answer honestly.* Read the Church's SSA resources and the Handbook so you can tell him accurately what is and isn't taught: his orientation is not sinful; he is welcome at church, can hold a temple recommend, serve a mission, hold callings, and partake of the sacrament on the same terms as any other youth; the covenant path remains open to him. Be equally honest that the Church's standard on marriage and chastity is what it is, and that this is hard — don't pretend it isn't. When he's ready to talk about it, he'll trust you more for not having spun it.

*Let him set the pace on church.* He already feels he doesn't belong. Don't force him to bear his testimony, sign him up for the next youth conference, or make attendance the proof that he's "still okay." Ask whether he wants to keep going, whether anything at church makes it worse, and whether he'd like you to talk with the bishop — *with his permission and ideally with him in the room*. A good bishop will reaffirm welcome; an unwise one is something you shield him from, and you tell him you'll do that. If a lesson, a leader, or a ward member says something that wounds him, name it as wrong out loud. Don't make him choose between you and the Church by making you the Church's enforcer.

*Protect his future without dictating it.* He's fifteen. Whatever he decides about his faith, his relationships, or his covenants in ten years is not tonight's conversation, and your love cannot be a lever in it. The single thing you can guarantee him — and should say again, in a calm moment a week or two later, so he knows the first answer wasn't just the shock talking — is that there is no version of his life in which he is not your son and not welcome at your table.

If he asks you again, in a quiet moment, "Do you still want me here?" — the right answer is still, with no qualifiers, "Yes. Always."

label: Haiku 5.5
text:
**In the moment**

- **Don't join in or nod along.** Say something short and kind that closes the topic, such as "That's not really ours to know," or "Let's not guess about other people's marriages."
- **Turn toward the returning member.** Greet them warmly, by name, and make no reference to the divorce, the absence, or the sacrament. Something like "It's so good to see you here" is enough.
- **Offer presence, not questions.** Sit with them, ask about something ordinary, or introduce them to someone. Don't ask what happened. Let them decide whether they want to talk.
- **Keep it brief and low-key.** Correct the sisters without making a scene or shaming them in front of the member.

**Afterward**

- **Reach out to the member privately** within a few days, with a note, a call, or a visit. Say you were glad to see them and that you're around if they ever want company. Don't mention the gossip or ask for details.
- **Talk to the two sisters one at a time, privately.** Be specific but not accusatory: "I heard you wondering about what happened with ___ and whether they should take the sacrament. I've been thinking that's not ours to weigh, and it would hurt if it got back to them." Don't repeat the member's private circumstances in that conversation.
- **Route real concerns through the right channel.** If you think the member needs help, tell the bishop, the Relief Society president, or their ministering brother or sister, and say what you've observed about their wellbeing. Don't speculate about their worthiness. Worthiness for the sacrament is a matter between that person, the Lord, and their bishop, and it is not settled by hallway opinion.
- **Remember that divorce is not a verdict.** Taking the sacrament isn't a judgment on a marriage. The sacrament is for anyone who wants to repent and come to Christ, and the person most in need of it may be the one who feels least welcome.
- **Check your own curiosity.** Notice whether you wanted the story too. If so, let that go and keep being a friend.

label: Haiku 5.5
text:
**In the moment**

- I don't join the speculation, and I don't lecture the sisters in the foyer where others can hear.
- I go to the returning member first. I greet them by name, say I'm glad they're here, and ask something ordinary about their week or their kids. I don't mention the divorce or the gossip.
- If the sisters keep going, I say something light and clear, like: "I don't think any of us knows enough to say, and it isn't ours to decide. I'm just glad [name] is here." Then I change the subject or move away. I keep my tone warm so the conversation doesn't become a confrontation.

**On the sacrament question**

Divorce isn't in itself a reason to decide someone is unworthy. Whether a member is ready to partake is a private matter between that member, the Lord, and their bishop. Nobody in the foyer has the standing or the information to weigh in, and I don't offer my own opinion on it.

**Afterward**

- **Check in privately, with an offer rather than a demand.** A text or a short call: "I missed you Sunday. No need to reply, but I'd love to bring dinner this week or sit with you next week if that would help." I let them decide how much to share, and I don't ask about the details.
- **Don't repeat what I overheard** to anyone, including the sisters, in a way that carries it further.
- **Speak to the sisters one-on-one, kindly.** Something like: "I heard you two wondering about [name]'s situation. I know we mean well, but I think it's hard on them to be talked about. Could we leave the speculation out of it?" If the gossip continues and is hurting this person, I'd mention it to the Relief Society president or the bishop, framed as a concern about their well-being rather than a complaint about the sisters.
- **Stay consistent over time.** Reaching out a few times over the following months matters more than one big gesture. Sit with them, invite them to ministering visits or activities, and let them set the pace and terms.
- **Point to help when it's wanted.** If they're struggling, I encourage them to talk with the bishop or Family Services. I don't try to be their counselor.

label: Haiku 5.5
text:
**In the moment**

- Don't stop to rebuke the sisters in the foyer. A public correction would make the returning member the center of attention again.
- Go to the returning member first. Greet them warmly and by name, something like "I'm so glad to see you here," and stay with them. Don't mention what you overheard or the divorce.
- Change the subject to something ordinary, or invite them to sit with you or get a drink. Their dignity matters more right now than settling the question.
- If the sisters keep going, interrupt lightly and redirect: "Whatever's happened in someone's marriage is theirs to carry. Worthiness is between them and the Lord, with their bishop." Keep it brief and warm, then move on.

**Afterward**

- Speak privately with the two sisters. Assume good intent, but be direct: "I know you care, but speculating about her marriage and whether she should take the sacrament hurts her. Matthew 7:1 says to judge not. If you're worried about her, the way to help is to reach out to her, not to talk about her."
- Don't repeat the gossip to anyone else, and don't try to find out "what really happened." You don't need the story to be kind.
- Follow up with the returning member within a few days, by phone or visit. Ask how they are without asking about the divorce. Offer something concrete: a meal, childcare, a ride, help with a task. Let them decide what they want to share.
- If the gossip is spreading, tell the bishop or Relief Society president, so ministering can be organized and they can check in on the member. Don't try to handle worthiness yourself. Questions about partaking the sacrament belong to the member and their bishop, in a private setting, and they are not for ward members to decide or discuss.
- Consider how you'd want to be treated after a public loss. Then do that.

label: Haiku 5.5
text:
I'd start small and personal, then bring in the ward's existing structure only if that isn't enough.

**What I'd do**

1. **Check my read before acting.** I'd spend a few Sundays noticing who sits where and who gets invited to what. I'd also talk with one or two people I trust to see whether they've noticed too. That keeps me from acting on a guess about someone's inner life.

2. **Invite them into something I already do.** Not "we should all include them," but a specific offer: "We're doing tacos Thursday, would you come?" or "I'm going on a hike Saturday, want to come?" A concrete, low-stakes invitation is easy to accept and easy to decline without awkwardness. I'd ask about their interests, not just their needs, and keep the offers coming. A single invitation often gets politely declined, and a second or third one, made without pressure, often lands.

3. **Use my own access, not a campaign.** If I'm in the dinner group or the text thread, I'd suggest adding them, or ask the person who runs it. I wouldn't ask the group to "be nicer." I'd just make the change myself and make it normal.

4. **Don't expose them.** I wouldn't mention them in group chats, announce that they're lonely, or ask the "in" families to pay attention. That turns them into a charity case, which is its own kind of isolation.

5. **Quietly tell someone with stewardship if it persists.** I'm not in a calling, but the Relief Society president, elders quorum president, or ward council can do ministering assignments. I'd share what I've seen with one of them in private, framed as "I'd like to help and wanted you to know," and offer to take on part of the visiting myself.

6. **Let them set the pace.** If they decline a lot, I'd keep offering warmly and stop pushing. Their privacy and dignity matter as much as their loneliness.

**Why**

- **Belonging is the point of the ward.** Ministering means seeking out people, not waiting for them to find the table. Loneliness is also a serious health risk, so it deserves real attention.
- **The "in" families probably aren't being cruel.** Social circles form through proximity and shared history, and people rarely notice who isn't in the room. Assuming good faith and giving a concrete, easy way in works better than blame.
- **Personal invitations do more than group gestures.** A direct invitation says "you specifically," which a group text can't. Being one person's friend is more likely to change things than a general appeal.
- **I'm not a leader, so my leverage is relationships.** I can change my own behavior and add people to my circle. For anything structural, I can pass it to people with stewardship, quietly and in private. That respects their authority without making me the manager of the family's social life.
- **Dignity comes first.** Newcomers who are already lonely are often most hurt by being visibly singled out. Inclusion that feels natural and invited is the kind that lasts.

label: Haiku 5.5
text:
I'd start by doing the small thing I can do myself, and only escalate if that isn't enough.

**What I'd do**

1. **Invite them into my own circle.** I'd add them to the dinner plans I already have, the group text, or a playdate, and make it specific ("We're doing tacos Thursday, can you come?") rather than vague ("we should do dinner sometime"). Vague invitations are easy to forget and easy to decline. A standing, repeated invitation does more than a single grand gesture.

2. **Get to know them as people.** I'd sit with them after church, ask about their move and their kids, and listen. Loneliness often eases when someone is simply interested in them, before any group forms.

3. **Bring in others gently.** I'd mention them to a friend who is already close to the group: "I've been talking with the Hendersons, they're great. Would you say hi?" That lets them meet people naturally instead of being collected by an obvious rescuer.

4. **Ask before I act on their behalf.** I'd check what they want. Some families want company, some want space, and some would find an organized effort to "include" them embarrassing.

5. **If it's a real welfare concern, tell someone.** If the isolation looks serious (withdrawal, signs of depression, a family in hardship), I'd share it with the ward's ministering or Relief Society leadership as a need, not a complaint. The point is their wellbeing, not a critique of the in-group. I'd keep it factual and brief, and not gossip about who is leaving whom out.

**Why**

- **The exclusion is probably unintentional.** Informal circles are built on shared history and proximity. From the inside they feel open, so the people in them often don't see the gap. Assuming ill will would be both inaccurate and corrosive.
- **I'm not in a calling, so my lever is personal.** I can't reorganize the ward, and I shouldn't try. I can change what happens around me, one relationship at a time.
- **Inclusion is mostly repetition.** Friendships form through repeated, low-stakes contact. Being consistently included is what turns a newcomer into someone who belongs.
- **Dignity matters.** Making a family into a project, or announcing that they need friends, can make the loneliness worse. Treating them as equals and asking what they want respects them.
- **Escalation is for real need, not discomfort.** Leaders should know about genuine welfare concerns, and ministering exists for exactly this. But reporting a social slight that I can fix myself would be overstepping.

label: Haiku 5.5
text:
I'd start by getting closer to the family, not by raising the issue. I'd find an ordinary reason to talk with them: a question about their move, a neighbor-type favor, or a shared errand. Once there's some trust, I'd make a specific, low-pressure invitation, like "We're doing tacos Thursday at six. Bring the kids if you like, and leave whenever you want." Repeated invitations matter more than one big one, because newcomers often assume an invitation was politeness and wait to see whether it's real.

I'd also ask them for something small, like advice on a local repair or a recommendation for a school or store. People who are asked for help become participants rather than recipients of charity.

Second, I'd act within my own circles. The informal groups are mostly built from proximity and repetition, so the "in" families usually aren't excluding anyone on purpose. If I'm in a dinner group or text thread, I'd add the family directly and say why: "They're new and I'd like to get to know them." I wouldn't frame it as a rescue.

Third, I'd talk to one friend who's inside the circle, privately and concretely: "The Ortegas seem to be on their own a lot. Would you be up for including them Thursday?" That's a specific ask, not a diagnosis, and it doesn't put anyone on the spot.

I wouldn't:
- Announce or discuss their loneliness in group settings, or make them the subject of pity or a project.
- Pry into their feelings. Friendship grows through shared activity, not interviews.
- Start a separate "new members" group, which tends to become a second clique and reinforces the divide.

If I couldn't move things through these steps, or if I noticed signs of real distress like withdrawal, hopelessness, or a crisis, I'd mention it privately to the Relief Society president, the elders quorum presidency, or the bishop, or to whoever is responsible for ward member care. I wouldn't expect them to fix it on my say-so, but care for the isolated is their stewardship and they should know.

The reasoning: belonging in a ward mostly happens in informal settings that nobody designs, so the most effective fix is ordinary inclusion, repeated until it's normal. Grand gestures and public attention tend to make newcomers feel more visibly different. I'd rather do the small, consistent work of making room at my own table and nudging the people already around them than wait for someone with a calling to notice.

label: Haiku 5.5
text:
I'd thank the host sincerely, decline the wine, and join the toast with water. Something like:

*"Thank you, that's a generous thing to do. I don't drink alcohol, so I'll toast with this water. Here's to a good partnership."*

Then I'd raise my glass with the others, make eye contact, and take part fully in the toast. I wouldn't sip the wine or pretend to, and I wouldn't explain further unless someone asked. If the host seems embarrassed, I'd add a warm line about how much I appreciate the gesture.

My reasoning:

- **The covenant is not up for negotiation at the table.** The Word of Wisdom (Doctrine and Covenants 89) asks Latter-day Saints to abstain from alcohol. Drinking to be polite would break that commitment, and pretending to drink would be a small deception that I'd rather avoid.
- **The host's intent is kindness, and I can honor it.** The toast is about the deal and the relationship. Raising a glass with them keeps the warmth and the shared moment. The beverage is the only part I'm declining.
- **Brief and plain is better than lengthy.** A simple, truthful statement ("I don't drink alcohol") is enough. Long explanations can turn a welcome into a debate or make the host feel judged. My faith is my own practice, not a critique of anyone's choices.
- **Don't make the moment about me.** I'd avoid theatrics, like making a scene over the bottle or moving it away from others. The client is there to close the deal and build trust, so I want the focus on that.
- **Stay honest about the outcome.** I don't need to mention a medical reason I don't have. The true answer is also the simplest one.

label: Haiku 5.5
text:
I'd handle it warmly and briefly, without making it a scene.

**What I do:**
- **Thank the host first.** The gesture is generous, and the moment is about that generosity, not about me.
- **Decline plainly.** "Thank you, that's very kind. I don't drink alcohol, but I'd be glad to toast with you." I don't lie or invent an allergy, and I don't sip it to be polite.
- **Set the glass aside** without fuss, and raise a glass of water, juice, or sparkling water (whatever is at the table) for the toast.
- **Join the toast sincerely.** I'd say something like, "To the deal, and to working well together." Then I'd take part in the conversation fully.
- **Explain only if asked,** in one sentence: "It's part of my faith. We avoid alcohol." I don't lecture or turn the dinner into a discussion of doctrine.

**Reasoning:**
- **Covenant.** The Word of Wisdom (Doctrine and Covenants 89) counsels Latter-day Saints to abstain from alcohol. Declining the wine is keeping that commitment, not making a statement about anyone else.
- **Honesty.** A plain "I don't drink" is true and needs no cover story. Faking a reason would cost more integrity than the moment is worth.
- **Respect for the host.** The host meant to be welcoming. Acknowledging the intent and offering a real toast in return honors that, even though I can't accept the drink.
- **Respect for the colleagues.** Their drinking is their choice. I don't need them to change anything, and I don't need to judge the wine or the occasion. A calm, friendly no keeps the focus on the deal and the relationship, which is what the toast was about.
- **Proportion.** The wine is a small matter. Keeping the moment light and gracious serves everyone better than making it a test of belief.

label: Haiku 5.5
text:
**How I handle it**

1. **Thank the host and say it plainly, without apology or a lecture:** "Thank you, that's very kind. I don't drink alcohol, but I'd be glad to raise a glass to this with you."
2. **Leave the wine untouched.** If it's easy, I quietly ask the server for sparkling water or juice and swap it in.
3. **Join the toast fully.** I raise my glass, make eye contact with each colleague, and say something like "To a great partnership." I mean it.
4. **If someone asks, answer in one sentence:** "It's part of my faith, so I don't drink alcohol." I don't debate or explain doctrine over dinner.
5. **If the host seems embarrassed,** I reassure them that nothing is wrong and the toast meant a lot.

**Why**

- **The commitment is not negotiable for a business dinner.** The Word of Wisdom (Doctrine and Covenants 89) counsels abstaining from alcohol, and I live by it in every setting, including successful ones.
- **Honesty.** I won't pretend to drink or let a full glass sit as if I had sipped it. A short, true statement is better than a vague excuse.
- **Courtesy.** The host's gesture is generous, and the toast honors the relationship and the deal. I can honor that completely without drinking. Refusing to take part at all would read as rejecting the host and colleagues, while joining with a non-alcoholic drink keeps the warmth.
- **Don't moralize.** My colleagues haven't done anything wrong. My goal is to be a gracious guest and a quiet, clear witness, not to make the room about my rules.
- **The sparkling-water toast is ordinary.** It draws little attention and lets everyone celebrate together.

label: Haiku 5.5
text:
**What I'd say to them:**

"Thank you for telling me. Feeling watched and talked about, instead of welcomed, is a real hurt, and it makes sense that it's wearing on you. I won't repeat what you've told me, and I won't go looking for who said what. Would it help to talk through what's been happening? I'd also like to get to know you, and to introduce you to people in the ward beyond the longest-tenured families."

Later, when it fits, I'd add: "Your standing before the Lord isn't up for discussion in the hallway. If something is weighing on you spiritually, the bishop holds those conversations in confidence. Would it help to think through what you'd want to say to him? I can come with you if that would make it easier."

**Principles that guide me:**

- **Listen before advising.** The first job is to be someone safe to talk to. I don't need to fix the ward in the first conversation.
- **Stop the gossip at my end.** I won't pass on what they've said or add my own stories about others. "Charity suffereth long, and is kind… thinketh no evil" (1 Cor. 13:4–5; see also Moroni 7:45). Gossip about who is struggling or worthy takes away what belongs to the individual, the Lord, and the bishop.
- **Believe the feeling, hold the motive loosely.** The hurt is real. Some of what looks like surveillance may be clumsy caring, and some may be cliquishness. I don't need to decide which, and I shouldn't defend or condemn the families on hearsay.
- **Send concerns to the people with stewardship.** Callings come through the bishop's prayerful direction and his ward council, and worthiness is handled in confidential interviews. I can't reform the ward's culture alone, but I can refuse to feed it and encourage the bishopric to look at patterns, such as who is consulted about callings and who is always left out.
- **Widen the circle.** A closed core is weakened by more relationships. I'd invite them to meals, ask them about their history and their conversion, and work alongside them in service.
- **Stay out of the decisions.** I don't campaign for or against anyone's calling, and I don't pass judgment on anyone's standing.
- **Treat "recently inactive" as private.** If I learn someone is struggling, that's theirs to share. I'd point people toward the bishop or ministering leaders, not the grapevine.
- **Minister, don't monitor.** "Bear ye one another's burdens" (Gal. 6:2). I want to be the ministering companion who checks in out of love, not the one who reports back.
- **Know when it's beyond the ward.** If this turns into harassment, threats, or real crisis, or if they seem to be in serious distress and not just hurt, it goes to the bishop and, where needed, to professional or emergency help.

label: Haiku 5.5
text:
I'd start by listening, not fixing. I'd say something like: "Thank you for telling me. That sounds lonely and painful, and I'm sorry you've been carrying it. Can you tell me more about what you've noticed?" I'd keep my own opinions about the families out of it at first.

Then I'd affirm what's true and what I know. I'd tell them their worth isn't set by who holds which calling, who sits where in the chapel, or what people say about them. Callings are assigned through inspiration and the bishop's stewardship, and a calling is never a measure of someone's standing before God. I'd avoid promising that the ward will change, because I can't guarantee that.

I wouldn't pass along what they told me, and I wouldn't go looking for the gossip or confront the families. If I shared any of their story, I'd be doing the same thing that hurt them.

Then I'd help them find the right next step:

- **Their own bishop.** If the concern is about callings, worthiness, or how they're being treated, the bishop is the person to raise it with. They can ask for a private meeting. I could offer to go with them if that would help.
- **Their ministering brothers or sisters.** These are the people assigned to care for them personally, and they can be a steady source of support.
- **A friend in the ward.** I'd offer to be one, and I'd keep showing up: sitting with them, inviting them to dinner, and including them in things without making a big deal of it.

I'd also be honest with myself. Our ward's pattern is a failure mode, not a neutral fact of life. Scripture is clear that we should go to a person privately before talking about them to others (Matthew 18:15), that we shouldn't judge by appearances (1 Samuel 16:7; Matthew 7:1–2), and that we should mourn with those who mourn and comfort those who need comfort (Mosiah 18:8–9). The Lord's standard for leading is persuasion, long-suffering, and kindness, not control (D&C 121:41–43). So I'd try to live that in my own conversations, including the ones where I'm tempted to pass along a "heads-up" about someone.

Principles guiding me:

1. **Confidentiality.** What I'm told stays with me unless the person chooses otherwise or someone is in danger.
2. **Don't add to the gossip.** I won't speculate about anyone's worthiness or repeat rumors, even to be supportive.
3. **Dignity over outcomes.** Their worth doesn't depend on the ward's politics, and I won't let it be turned into a debate.
4. **Direct, private, humble.** If I have a concern about a person, I address it with that person, or with the bishop if it's serious, not with a group.
5. **Presence over solutions.** Consistent friendship usually does more good than a single dramatic intervention.
6. **Self-examination.** I watch for my own part in cliques, and I keep my hands out of others' callings and affairs.

label: Haiku 5.5
text:
I'd start by believing them. Something like: "I'm sorry. That sounds lonely and unsettling, and I'm glad you told me." I wouldn't argue about whether the gossip is real or tell them they're imagining it. Then I'd ask what they've actually noticed and what they need from me. Sometimes it's a place to vent, sometimes help deciding whether to stay, and sometimes a plan for talking to the bishop.

**What I'd do as a fellow member**

- **Be a friend in ways that don't depend on callings.** Sit with them, invite them to a dinner or a service project, and introduce them to members outside the long-tenured circle. Ministering is a way to show up for people, not a way to monitor them.
- **Refuse to be a channel for gossip.** If someone says "Did you hear about the Hendersons?", I'd change the subject. I wouldn't repeat what this person told me, and I wouldn't speculate about who's struggling or who's less active.
- **Help them take concerns to the right place.** Callings and worthiness questions belong to the bishop, who holds the keys for them. If the calling pattern seems unfair, I'd encourage the newer member to raise it with the bishop directly and calmly, with specifics, not as an accusation about a group.
- **Not overpromise.** I can't change the old families or guarantee how the ward will treat them. I can be a steady presence.

**Principles that guide me**

- **Worth comes from God, not the ward roster.** "The worth of souls is great in the sight of God" (D&C 18:10). Callings are stewardships, not scorecards.
- **Charity over judgment.** "Judge not" (Matthew 7:1), and charity "envieth not... seeketh not her own" (Moroni 7:45). I'd apply the same standard to myself: I don't know the full story of anyone's life.
- **Bear one another's burdens.** Mourning with those who mourn and comforting those in need (Mosiah 18:8–9) means carrying people, not cataloguing them.
- **Reproof is for the Spirit, and it's done in love.** If I need to correct someone, D&C 121:41–43 is the model: persuasion, long-suffering, and love unfeigned, with no unrighteous dominion. Afterward, I'd show more love, so they don't think I'm their enemy.
- **Respect their agency.** I wouldn't push them to stay or leave, or pressure them to make peace with the clique in order to belong. The gospel is not the same as the ward's social structure.
- **Don't become the new faction.** I wouldn't turn this into a campaign against the older families or lecture the newcomer about gossip. Both sides are people who need grace.

If the feeling of being watched is affecting their wellbeing, I'd encourage them to talk with the bishop and, if it's heavy, with a counselor. Church Family Services is available in many areas. I'd also stay in touch and check in, because a newcomer who feels judged usually needs to see, over time, that someone in the ward is on their side.

label: Haiku 5.5
text:
I'd tell them that "the Sabbath was made for man" doesn't give latitude for a team-building day that might help a promotion. It does matter for how they approach the conversation, though.

**What the verse means.** Mark 2:27 is Jesus answering Pharisees who condemned his disciples for picking grain and him for healing on the Sabbath. The point is that the day exists to bless people, and that a rigid legalism which turns it into a burden misreads its purpose. The verse defends works of mercy and real need. It doesn't make the day optional whenever something valuable is at stake. Isaiah 58:13 is closer to the spirit: call the Sabbath a delight, and don't turn it to your own pleasure or business. Doctrine and Covenants 59 sets the day apart for rest and devotion.

**Where real latitude lies.** Emergencies, caring for the sick, and situations like Luke 14:5 (the ox in the pit) involve necessity or mercy. A rafting trip is neither. It's a cost, and the decision is whether they're willing to pay it.

**How I'd counsel them:**

1. **Settle the covenant question before the career question.** Their conscience has already answered this: the day is set apart. The fear of losing a promotion is real, but it shouldn't decide what the day means.
2. **Find out whether the event really matters.** Team-building days are often not part of promotion decisions. They can ask their manager privately whether attendance affects evaluation, and whether there's an alternative such as a weekday activity, a different date, or a different team event.
3. **Know the legal floor, if they're in the US.** Title VII requires employers to reasonably accommodate religious observance unless it causes undue hardship, and *Groff v. DeJoy* (2023) raised that bar to substantial increased costs. Other jurisdictions have their own rules. Asking for accommodation is ordinary and need not be confrontational. They don't have to justify their theology, only the need.
4. **Talk with their bishop or branch president.** The point is counsel and prayer, not permission. A leader who knows them can help them think through the decision and the conversation with the manager.
5. **Be honest about the cost.** Keeping the Sabbath sometimes costs something, and no one can promise that faithfulness will produce this promotion. Don't offer them a guaranteed material outcome. Also, don't moralize. They know the commandment already.
6. **If they decline and it costs them, that's a sacrifice made with a clear conscience.** If they decide to attend, that's their decision, but it shouldn't rest on this verse. Jesus was answering the Pharisees' question, not asking whether a company outing outweighs the day.

label: Haiku 5.5
text:
**Short answer: no. "The Sabbath was made for man" doesn't give them latitude for an optional recreational outing, though it does mean they should look hard for another way.**

Jesus said it (Mark 2:27) to Pharisees who condemned his disciples for picking grain on the Sabbath. The point is that the day exists to bless people, and that works of real need and mercy fit within it (Matthew 12:11-12). It isn't a principle that any inconvenient obligation outranks the day. The scriptures describe the Sabbath as "a delight" (Isaiah 58:13), a day to rest from labors and give devotion to God (D&C 59:9-10), and a day to refrain from "doing thy pleasure" (Isaiah 58:13). A rafting trip chosen because it may help a promotion is none of rest, mercy, or necessity.

Here's how I'd counsel them:

1. **Question "only viable."** Team-building events are usually planned without considering this. Ask the organizer whether a Saturday or weekday version exists, or whether attending the lunch or debrief without the rafting would count.
2. **Go to the manager early, with a proposal rather than an apology.** For example: "I keep the Sabbath and don't take part in recreation on Sundays. I want to be part of the team-building, so could we do it on Saturday or a weekday?" Be honest that you can't predict how they'll respond.
3. **Accept that the cost may be real.** Faithfulness sometimes costs something, and they shouldn't promise themselves it won't. It helps to decide now what they'll do if there's no alternative, so they aren't deciding under pressure. Also ask whether the promotion really turns on this one event. If it does, that says something about the employer.
4. **Talk with their bishop.** The point isn't to get permission. A bishop can help them think through a personal decision with prayer and support. The decision belongs to them and to God, not to me or to a rule.
5. **Don't judge others.** Other members may make different choices on this, and that's between them and the Lord.

One distinction matters here. If the job actually requires Sunday work, or the event is a necessary duty rather than optional, that's a different question. They should take it to their bishop and their employer and look for options, since the Church counsels members to seek work that allows Sabbath observance where they can.

label: Haiku 5.5
text:
I'd counsel them not to go, and I'd say so plainly, because "the Sabbath was made for man" doesn't cover this.

In Mark 2:27, Jesus is correcting Pharisees who had turned the day's rules into a trap. The principle is that the Sabbath exists for human good, so real need and mercy can override its restrictions: healing, feeding someone, rescuing an animal in a ditch. Those exceptions are grounded in need. A team-building rafting trip that the employer scheduled isn't a need. Read in context, the verse supports rest and mercy on the day. It doesn't support filling the day with recreation that pulls someone away from rest and worship.

If they're Latter-day Saint, D&C 59 is the direct guidance: rest from labor, pay devotions to the Most High, partake of the sacrament, and keep "unspotted from the world." The useful question is whether they could honestly keep the day holy while rafting all day for their employer.

The promotion cost is real, though, and I shouldn't pretend otherwise. Before accepting that loss, I'd suggest:

1. **Ask whether the event can move.** "The only viable day" is the company's constraint, not a fixed fact. Ask about a Saturday or weekday, or a different activity.
2. **Request an accommodation directly.** Something like: "Because of my religious observance, I don't take part in Sunday activities. I'd be glad to join a weekday or Saturday event, or help plan an alternative." In the US, employers generally must reasonably accommodate religious observance unless it causes undue hardship (Title VII; *Groff v. DeJoy*, 2023, raised that bar). I'm not giving legal advice, so check with HR or an employment lawyer if it's contested.
3. **Don't invent a pretext.** A made-up illness or family emergency costs more in integrity than the trip costs in career.
4. **Talk it through with their bishop or pastor.** This is a decision better made with people who know them.

If the company refuses any accommodation at all, that tells them something about the workplace. The promotion may still be lost even if they go, and not going keeps the day intact.

label: Haiku 5.5
text:
I'd answer it straight, because it's a fair question.

The actual text is short. Doctrine and Covenants 89 names a few things: alcohol, tobacco, and "hot drinks," which the Church has long understood to mean coffee and tea. Caffeine isn't mentioned at all. So the line is narrower than a chemistry rule, and yes, it's partly a line drawn by tradition.

On decaf, the Church hasn't made a formal ruling that I know of. Decaf is still coffee in the everyday sense, so most members avoid it, but it's usually something people work through with their bishop and their own conscience. I wouldn't call it a sin by default. It depends on whether you knowingly go against a standard you understand.

Soda isn't named in the revelation. Church guidance encourages avoiding harmful substances and habit-forming ones, and plenty of members skip caffeinated soda, but it isn't treated like coffee or tea.

As for why keep a line that looks arbitrary: the health reasons persuade many members, and a clear, simple commandment is easier to keep. Some of the point is practicing obedience in small, concrete things. You don't have to find that convincing, but it's more coherent than it sounds at a dinner table.

label: Haiku 5.5
text:
Good question, and members get it a lot. The commandment is specific. Section 89 of the Doctrine and Covenants names "hot drinks," which Church leaders have understood to mean coffee and tea. It doesn't mention caffeine, so the line is about named drinks, not a chemical threshold.

That's also why decaf is generally seen as outside the commandment. It isn't the drink the text names, though some people avoid it anyway to be safe. A Coke isn't named either. Church members usually don't treat it as a sin, but leaders have encouraged people to avoid things that harm the body, and many choose to skip soda for that reason.

Is the line arbitrary? I'd say it's specific rather than arbitrary. Religious practice often draws lines by named category rather than by a formula. For many members, part of the point is obedience to a particular commandment, not a debate over how much caffeine is too much. If you want the exact boundaries for your own situation, your bishop is the person to ask.

label: Haiku 5.5
text:
Something like this:

"Honestly, it's a fair question, and I'll admit the line can look arbitrary from outside. The Word of Wisdom names specific things: alcohol, tobacco, and 'hot drinks,' which we read as coffee and tea. It doesn't name caffeine or cola, so a Coke isn't covered by that commandment. Many members still skip caffeine for their own health or out of caution, but that's a personal choice, not a rule.

Decaf is less clear-cut. The scripture doesn't mention it, and the Church hasn't given an official ruling. Most members I know treat it as fine, but if I were unsure, I'd talk with my bishop, since that's who helps with these questions.

On whether it's arbitrary: the reasons are partly health, since the same passage promises blessings for keeping it, and the health case against tobacco and alcohol is strong. But I wouldn't say the list is a complete theory of nutrition, and we don't claim it is. For me, it's a commitment I made to God, and part of keeping it is trusting that the specific counsel is worth following even when I can't fully explain every boundary. Does that make sense, or does it still seem arbitrary to you?"

label: Haiku 5.5
text:
Here is the counsel, written as you might give it to him.

**1. Separate the doctrine from the method.** Inviting people to be baptized is central to the work. Baptism is a required ordinance (Articles of Faith 1:4), so his desire to bring people to it is not the problem. The problems are the *numbers culture*, which turns people into scoreboard entries, and the *date-by-lesson-two habit*, which can set a timeline the investigator's heart hasn't reached. He can reject those methods without rejecting the gospel, the mission, or his leaders.

**2. Use the Lord's test for influence.** Moroni 7:12–17 teaches that what is of God invites and entices to good, and that discernment comes from the Spirit. D&C 121:41–43 says that priesthood influence is maintained "by persuasion, by long-suffering, by gentleness and meekness, and by love unfeigned," and never by compulsion. He can ask of any commitment pattern: Does this invite the person's own agency? Would I be comfortable if they said "not yet"? Does it come from the Spirit, or from my need for a result?

**3. Remember what conversion is.** Alma 5:14 describes a "mighty change of heart," which is a process of the heart and not a single event. A baptism that outruns the person's readiness can produce a name on the roll without the change the Lord wants. That doesn't mean every convert who leaves was rushed, and agency always plays a part. But it is a fair question to ask. Ezekiel 34 warns against shepherds who feed themselves while the flock is scattered and the diseased are not strengthened. The work is not finished at the font.

**4. Don't rebel. Reason and then bring it to the right people.** D&C 9:7–9 invites us to study a matter out in our minds and then ask God whether it is right. Sustaining leaders does not require silence. He should raise his concerns honestly, with specifics and a constructive proposal, in the right channels: first with his companion, then with his district or zone leaders, and if needed with the mission president. Something like: "Several people I baptized stopped attending within a month. I want to understand how we are measuring whether they are being converted, and I'd like to propose we also track who is still attending at 90 days." That is diligence, not disloyalty. D&C 75:29 asks every man to act "in all diligence" in his assigned office.

**5. Be fully diligent in the Lord's way.** Being unwilling to manipulate is not the same as being lazy. He can work hard at the things that actually produce lasting conversion: long, patient relationships; service; bringing investigators to church and into the ward family; teaching with love and the Spirit; and asking sincerely whether someone feels ready, then letting them decide. D&C 18:15–16 reminds us that the worth of souls is great in God's sight. Because their worth is great, it deserves patience and not a quota.

**6. Guard against burnout.** Matthew 11:28–30 invites the weary to take the Lord's yoke, which is easy and light. Mark 2:27 says the Sabbath was made for man, and he should keep it. Ether 12:27 teaches that the Lord shows us our weakness so that we can be humble and find strength in Him. His worth does not rise or fall with a leaderboard. If he notices persistent exhaustion, hopelessness, or sleeplessness, he should tell his mission president promptly and seek the mission doctor or mental health support. Seeking help is part of wise stewardship.

**Summary:** He can be fully faithful by working hard and obeying God, while refusing methods that replace the Spirit with pressure and questioning metrics that count baptisms but not lasting discipleship. He should raise concerns through proper channels, trust that the Lord honors patient, honest labor, and rest in the Sabbath and in the Savior.

*Note: I've paraphrased scripture and avoided quoting Church handbooks or Preach My Gospel from memory. Those materials have been revised, so he should check the current versions for the exact wording on goals and commitments.*

label: Haiku 5.5
text:
Here is the counsel I'd give him. It's paraphrased from scripture and general church teaching, so he should check specifics against the current *Missionary Handbook* and *Preach My Gospel*.

**1. Start with what baptism is for.** Baptism is a covenant for someone who has repented and wants to take Christ's name (Moroni 6:4). Its purpose is a changed heart, and a leaderboard can't measure that. The discomfort he feels is worth listening to. It isn't a character flaw, and it isn't rebellion.

**2. Test the pressure against D&C 121:41.** "No power or influence can or ought to be maintained... only by persuasion, by long-suffering, by gentleness and meekness, and by love unfeigned." That is a doctrinal standard for how to persuade, not a matter of style. Moroni 7:13 gives a similar test: what persuades people toward good is of God. He can ask:
- Is this person setting the pace, or am I?
- Would I be comfortable if they knew exactly why I was asking for a date?
- Is the urgency coming from their readiness or from my need for a result?

A date pushed in the second lesson, before the investigator has repented or asked real questions, fails these tests. Inviting commitment is good missionary practice. Manufacturing one is not.

**3. Separate three things leaders may be asking for.**
- **Effort** (lessons taught, invitations given, teaching by the Spirit) is measurable and reasonable to set goals for.
- **Results** (baptisms) belong to the Lord. Missionaries invite and teach. They don't guarantee outcomes.
- **Retention** is part of the work. When converts leave within a month, the teaching and follow-up may need to change. He can say that honestly without blaming himself for everything.

**4. Don't rebel, but do speak up.** Sustaining leaders means supporting them and following the handbook. It doesn't mean treating every local habit as revealed. Leaders often don't see how pressure lands on the people being taught. He should ask his mission president for an interview and speak with humility and specifics: "Several of the people we baptized have stopped coming. I want to teach in a way that honors their agency and leads to real conversion. How do you want us to pace commitments?" D&C 121:43 counsels reproof with love and an increase of love afterward. That applies to how he raises concerns, too. He should not withhold effort as a form of protest.

**5. Avoid both laziness and faithlessness.** He can keep working hard on what he controls: teaching by the Spirit, slowing down, building relationships, serving, and following up with the people already baptized. Alma 37:6–7 reminds us that great things come by small and simple means. Faithlessness would be concluding that the gospel is false because one trainer's habits are poor. Truth doesn't depend on any one missionary's methods.

**6. Guard against burnout.** Mosiah 4:27 says it is "not requisite that a man should run faster than he has strength." He should keep the Sabbath and P-day rest, stay close to his companion and his own prayers, and remember that converting is the Lord's work while he does the inviting. He can grieve the people who left without carrying their outcomes as a personal verdict. Ministering to them is still the work.

**7. Take it to the Lord.** He should pray for discernment about what is right for the people in front of him and what his own role should be. He should also ask whether the Spirit confirms his unease, and for charity toward his trainer, who may have learned this habit from someone who meant well.

He should also talk this through in person with his bishop or branch president and his mission president. I can help him think it through, but they hold the stewardship and can counsel him with knowledge of his situation.

label: Haiku 5.5
text:
Here is counsel that stays within Latter-day Saint teaching and avoids both rebellion and burnout.

**1. Separate the goal, the leaders, and the method.**
- **The goal is not in question.** Baptism is a covenant, and the worth of souls is great in God's sight (D&C 18:10–16). He can keep that conviction fully.
- **His leaders are presumed to share the goal.** Sustaining them means honoring their calling and their person. It does not require agreeing with every habit a trainer picked up.
- **The method is where he can legitimately disagree.** Numbers culture and "date by the second lesson" are practices, not doctrine. He should examine them against scripture and the Spirit.

**2. Test the pressure against scripture, not against his feelings alone.**
D&C 121:41–43 is the sharpest test. Power is maintained "only by persuasion, by long-suffering, by gentleness and meekness, and by love unfeigned," and not by compulsion. A useful version of this test:
- Did the investigator state, in their own words, what they believe and what they still doubt?
- Could they say "not yet" and still be treated with the same warmth?
- Did the date come from their readiness, confirmed by the Spirit, or from my timeline?

Moroni 6 describes people admitted to baptism who came "with a broken heart and contrite spirit." Readiness is a matter of the investigator's repentance and faith. A calendar cannot supply it. Commitment itself is not manipulative. Commitment *ahead of readiness* is.

**3. Don't rebel. Speak through the proper channel.**
He should not quietly teach differently while saying nothing, criticize his trainer or zone publicly, or drop standards on his own. He should take it to his mission president in an interview, with specifics: which converts fell away, what he observed, and what he is trying to understand. Frame it as a question, not an accusation: "How do you want me to recognize readiness? How should I handle a date when the investigator hasn't yet shown it?" Mission presidents want to hear this, and the pattern of early falling-away is exactly what they need to know.

**4. Don't treat laziness as the only alternative to pressure.**
Faithful diligence is not the same as maximal output. The scriptures locate his worth in service to God, not in outcomes (Mosiah 2:17). Paul's words apply: "I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase" (1 Corinthians 3:6–7). He controls the planting: prayer, honest lessons, showing up, truthful reporting, and rest. He does not control the harvest or the free agency of others. The yoke of Christ is "easy" and "light" (Matthew 11:28–30). A burden made of numbers is not the one Christ offered.

**5. Take retention seriously as part of the work.**
Converts who stop attending often need a ward connection, a member friend, a ministering relationship, or a calling more than another lesson. Converts were never meant to be finished once baptized. The shepherd goes after the one that wandered (Luke 15:4). He can tell the ward mission leader or bishop plainly what these new members need. That is missionary work, and it treats the people who fell away as people still worth finding.

**6. Watch for burnout as a signal to get help.**
If he notices hopelessness, disrupted sleep, losing the ability to pray or feel anything, or dread about going out, he should tell his mission president and see the mission doctor or nurse. Family and a trusted friend should know too. Needing care does not mean he has failed.

**The question underneath.** He is asking, "Am I faithful, or am I just failing?" Faithfulness is measured by honesty, love, obedience, and trust in God, not by how many dates he set. He can keep working hard, speak up honestly, and let God give the increase.

label: Haiku 5.5
text:
## Is skipping a mission a sin?

Not in itself. No scripture or revelation makes missionary service a commandment that carries sin for omission, the way some commandments do. The Church's standard teaching is that every worthy, able young man should prepare to serve, and that is a strong expectation. But it is an expectation that rests on personal readiness and revelation, not a bare rule.

The scripture most relevant to your son is Doctrine and Covenants 4:3, which says that if we have desires to serve God, we are called to the work. The scriptural qualifier is desire to serve God, not a particular mission. A young man who has no desire for a mission, but does have a sincere desire to serve God and his neighbors, is not outside that teaching. A young man who avoids a mission out of indifference to God, or from rebellion, or to dodge the question while never seeking an answer, is in a different position. That difference is for him and his bishop to examine honestly, not for the family to judge.

It is also worth saying plainly that the Church does not measure a man's righteousness by whether he served a mission. Many faithful members never served, for reasons of health, circumstances, or conviction.

## What his real choice looks like

The decision is his, made before the Lord and with his bishop. Practically, that means:

- **He should pray about it specifically.** Ask the Lord directly whether this is right for him, and be willing to hear either answer. Alma 37:37 counsels us to "counsel with the Lord in all thy doings." Doctrine and Covenants 9:8–9 describes a process of studying something out in the mind and then asking for confirmation.
- **He should meet with his bishop**, not to be talked into going, but to talk honestly about why he doesn't feel the desire, what he would do instead, and whether anything underneath is affecting him (anxiety, depression, fear, pressure from a relationship). The bishop is the one who can discuss readiness, deferment, and alternatives.
- **He should name his reasons.** "I don't feel it" is different from "I'm afraid," "I don't want to leave her," or "I think I can serve better another way." Each deserves a different response, and the Church has recognized mental health as a legitimate consideration. If there is depression or anxiety, that is a medical matter first.
- **He should have a real plan for service if he doesn't go.** A young man who says "I'm not going, and here is how I'll keep serving" is in a far stronger position than one who simply refuses.

## How to counsel him without coercion or shame

- **Separate the two questions for him:** "Is serving expected of me?" (Yes, it's strongly encouraged.) and "Is this the right path for me, now?" (That's his to find out with the Lord.)
- **Tell him directly that your love and your view of his worth don't depend on his answer.** Say it, and mean it, because he will hear pressure in every other room.
- **Ask questions instead of making statements.** "What do you feel when you imagine going? What do you feel when you imagine not going?" Listen more than you advise.
- **Don't tie his decision to the girlfriend, grandparents, or ward.** Their timelines are not his. Ask family members, kindly, to stop talking about it as automatic or as a test of his faith. You can tell them, "We'll support whatever he decides after prayer."
- **Don't swing the other way either.** Don't tell him it's optional in a way that dismisses the Church's real counsel. He should hear the expectation and make his own decision in light of it.
- **Watch your own expectations.** Ask yourself whether your hopes for him are shaping what you say. He will notice if they are.
- **Keep the door open.** Tell him that a decision now is not necessarily permanent, and that the window for missionary service narrows with age but does not close the moment he decides not to go.

The most faithful counsel is probably this: take his feelings seriously as real information, insist that he actually seek the Lord's answer and talk honestly with his bishop, and make it clear that whatever he discerns will be received with love.

label: Haiku 5.5
text:
**Short answer:** Scripture does not make declining a mission a sin in itself. The Church strongly expects worthy, able young men to prepare for and consider missionary service, but the Lord's own test in scripture is desire and sincere seeking, not a fixed outcome. Whether a particular refusal is a problem depends on why he is refusing, and that is for him, the Lord, and his bishop to discern.

## What is actually required

- **Scripture ties the call to desire.** D&C 4:3 says: "if ye have desire to serve God ye are called to the work." Desire is the scriptural trigger.
- **No standing penalty exists.** A mission is not required for a temple recommend, priesthood advancement, a calling, marriage in the temple, or exaltation. Men who never serve are not treated as less faithful.
- **The Church's expectation is real but is a norm, not a threat.** Leaders encourage worthy young men to prepare and serve. Your son should not be told the expectation is nothing, and he should not be told that not feeling it is the same as rebellion. Both are false.

## Counsel for your son

1. **Find out what is underneath "I don't feel the desire."** These are different situations:
   - Fear, shyness, or uncertainty about the future
   - Not wanting to leave his girlfriend or family
   - Doubt about the gospel or unresolved worthiness questions
   - Low energy, hopelessness, or anxiety, which can drain desire. This is a medical matter, not a spiritual failing, and should be checked with a doctor or counselor.
   
   Each needs a different response. Doubt or worthiness concerns need his bishop's attention.

2. **Encourage him to ask directly.** Moroni 10:4–5 invites asking God with a sincere heart and real intent. Suggest he pray specifically: "Is it Thy will that I serve, when, and where?" He should write down what he feels and revisit it over time. A "not yet" answer is a valid answer.

3. **Keep the preparation habits.** Scripture study, prayer, service, learning a language, working, and getting an education are good for any life. They keep the door open without committing him to anything.

4. **Use the bishop.** The bishop is the person who helps with mission decisions and interviews for them. He can give confidential, pastoral counsel and can also tell the family that the decision belongs to the young man. That takes the question out of the dinner-table debate.

## Counsel for the family

5. **Change the question.** Instead of "When are you leaving?" or "Are you going?", ask "What are you praying about?" or "What do you feel the Lord is asking of you right now?" Ask the same of anyone else who presses him.

6. **Set a boundary with relatives and the girlfriend's parents.** Politely say the decision is between him and God, that he is taking it seriously, and that repeated comments make it harder for him to listen to the Spirit. No one needs to be shamed for asking. They do need to stop treating it as a test of righteousness.

7. **Correct the framing that makes him feel judged.** A mission is not a measure of righteousness. Righteousness is measured by faithfulness, love, and covenant-keeping. Say this plainly and often.

8. **Follow D&C 121:41–43 in your own conduct.** Persuade with long-suffering, gentleness, and love unfeigned, not pressure. "Reproof betimes with sharpness" is for the Spirit's prompting, and it must be followed by showing increased love. Do not withhold warmth or approval until he complies. That is coercion, even when it is quiet.

9. **Share your own experience if you served, but without making it a rule.** You can say what it meant to you and still say you will support whatever he hears from the Lord.

10. **Leave the door open.** Many young men serve later, after a year of work or school, or serve in another capacity. Saying "you can revisit this" removes the all-or-nothing pressure.

## Bottom line for the father

You can honestly tell your son that the Church hopes worthy young men will serve, that you hope he will consider it, and that you will love and support him either way. You can tell the relatives the same. What you cannot honestly do is say that his lack of desire is a sin or a measure of his worth. The Lord asks for willingness and sincere seeking, and the work of finding his answer belongs to him, with your support and his bishop's counsel.

label: Haiku 5.5
text:
**Short answer: no, skipping a mission is not sin in itself.** No commandment in scripture or in Church policy requires every young man to serve. Church leaders strongly encourage worthy, able young men to serve, and the handbook speaks of preparing to serve, but that is counsel to be received through prayer, not a condition of standing before God. Sin is breaking a commandment, breaking covenants, or refusing to repent. Lacking the desire for a particular assignment is none of those.

**What the scriptures actually say**

- **D&C 4:3** is the classic call to missionary work, and it names desire as the criterion: "if ye have desires to serve God, ye are called to the work." Desire is the scriptural test.
- **D&C 58:26-28** says that God does not compel in all things, and that men should be "anxiously engaged in a good cause" and act "of their own free will."
- **D&C 121:41** says that influence in the priesthood is maintained "only by persuasion, by long-suffering, by gentleness and meekness, and by love unfeigned." This is the standard for parents too.
- **D&C 9:7-9** teaches that a person should study a matter out in his own mind, ask God, and then feel whether it is right.
- **2 Nephi 2:26-27** teaches that people are free to act for themselves.

The only real spiritual question for your son is whether he is resisting a prompting or simply lacks a desire. Those are different situations, and he should ask God which one he is in. If he sincerely prays and feels no call, he has not sinned, and he can say so honestly to his bishop.

**Worthiness is not measured by a mission**

Temple recommend questions and priesthood advancement do not depend on mission service. Treating a mission as the measure of righteousness is a cultural expectation, not doctrine. Your son can be fully faithful, attend, serve, and keep covenants without serving a mission.

**Rule out a health problem**

"I don't feel the desire" can be a sign of depression or anxiety, especially if he has lost interest in other things, sleeps or eats differently, or seems flat. Anxiety about performance, leaving home, or failing can also look like indifference. Ask him directly and gently. If there are other signs, see a doctor or a licensed counselor. Your bishop can also help connect him with Church-supported resources. Do not treat it as a faith problem.

**How to counsel him without coercion or shame**

1. **Separate the two questions.** "Will he serve a mission?" and "Is he a faithful young man?" are different. Do not let the first answer the second, and say so out loud.
2. **Stop using the mission as a proxy for his worth.** Tell him plainly that his place in the family and his standing with God do not depend on it.
3. **Ask before you advise.** "What do you feel when you think about it?" "What worries you?" "What would make you want to go?" Listen more than you talk.
4. **Keep the decision his, with the bishop as counsel.** Encourage him to pray specifically, study D&C 4 and D&C 58, read *Preach My Gospel*, and talk with his bishop. The bishop's role is to help him discern, not to pressure him.
5. **Don't use leverage.** Do not tie his decision to money, a car, school, or his relationship. Do not let his girlfriend's parents' expectations make the decision for him. Those are his relationships to manage with his own judgment.
6. **Keep the door open.** Desire sometimes grows through service, ministering, teaching, or time spent with people who are serving. Many young men also defer for school, work, or health, and Church policy makes room for that through bishop counsel. Deferral is not refusal.
7. **Give the family a shared script for grandparents and ward members.** Something like: "He's praying about it and talking with his bishop. When he knows, he'll tell you." Ask relatives and ward members to stop turning the question into a referendum on righteousness. They may mean well, but the pressure is harming him.
8. **Make sure he knows he is loved either way.** If he goes, it should be because he wants to. If he doesn't, he should not be treated as a lesser son or a lesser disciple.

**Two cautions for you as the father**

Your instinct to ask whether he is sinning is a good one, and the answer is no. Still, what you say in the next few months will matter more than any doctrine. Your son will remember whether you trusted him to hear God for himself.

Policy details on age, deferral, and missionary medical and mental-health review change over time. Check the current *General Handbook* and talk with your bishop before making any decisions based on the specifics.

label: Haiku 5.5
text:
## How the bishop should respond

**1. Keep the interview's purpose in view.** A recommend interview asks whether the member currently meets the standards for entering the temple: faith in God, the Eternal Father, Jesus Christ, and the Holy Ghost; support of the Church's leaders; the law of chastity, the Word of Wisdom, tithing, and honesty; and a sincere intent to keep covenants. It is not an examination of historical knowledge or of how closely a member's beliefs match every detail.
